case_annotation: The 'is a surviving spouse' flag does not create qualifying-surviving-spouse status. IRC §2(a) requires the filer to maintain a home for a dependent child, and none is listed, so the head files as single. Under single status, the $25,000/$34,000 thresholds make $18,542.70 of Social Security taxable, so AGI is $50,437.11. The post-OBBBA single standard deduction is $16,100 plus the $2,050 aged add-on, for $18,150, and the $6,000 senior deduction also applies. That leaves $26,287.11 of taxable income, taxed under the 2026 single brackets: 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above it, for $2,906.45. Most wrong answers made one of three errors: they used joint-style QSS thresholds and deductions, assumed the TCJA sunset (personal exemption and a 15% bracket), or left out the $6,000 senior deduction.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Texas Medicaid eligibility at age 77 requires qualification through an aged Medicaid pathway; age alone does not establish a qualifying category. This person has no Medicaid eligibility category, receives no SSI, and has MAGI income of 3.98 times FPL, so the immigration-status requirement does not create eligibility by itself.

Employee payroll taxes apply to wage and salary compensation, not to Social Security retirement benefits, pensions, IRA distributions, interest, or veterans benefits. Because the household reports no wages or other employee compensation, the employee Social Security and Medicare tax base is zero and payroll tax is $0.

Every model assumed the TCJA expired after 2025. They restored personal exemptions and a pre-TCJA-sized standard deduction of roughly $12,700 to $16,600. In fact, P.L. 119-21 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, July 2025) made the TCJA structure permanent: personal exemptions stay at $0, and the 2026 joint standard deduction is $32,200. That basic deduction alone is larger than the couple's AGI of $31,402.25. The AGI is $29,064 in wages plus $2,338.25 of taxable Social Security, under the 50% tier. The deduction grows further with the $1,650-per-spouse aged addition and the $6,000-per-senior deduction for both spouses, so taxable income is $0 and tax is $0. Four models got AGI right and left only a small positive taxable income because of the wrong deduction regime. grok-build-0.1 also overstated taxable Social Security by applying the 85% tier.

The trap is which Medicaid pathway a 71-year-old can use: Virginia's MAGI categories (expansion adults, parents, pregnant individuals) are closed to the head both by age and by income at 2.05x FPL, leaving only the SSI-linked aged pathway, which requires actually passing SSI's income and asset tests. Applying SSI counting rules to $15,225 of Social Security and $29,064 of wages leaves roughly $29,700 of annual countable income, so SSI is 0 and the aged category does not attach, yielding medicaid_category = NONE. All four wrong models skipped that income test — treating age 65+, Medicare Savings Program status, or unquantified disregards as sufficient on their own.

Employee FICA applies to the head's full $29,064 of wages despite the head's age. Social Security tax is $1,801.97 and Medicare tax is $421.43, which sum to $2,223.39; there is no Additional Medicare Tax and the spouse has no taxable wages.

SNAP first applies the gross-income eligibility limit to this two-person household. Its $44,289 annual gross income exceeds the applicable 2026 limit, so the calculation ends with no eligibility and deductions cannot produce a benefit.

The spouse is 69, which excludes them from Virginia's ACA expansion adult group (ages 19-64) and from every other MAGI category, and the household's Medicaid MAGI of $44,289 ($29,064 wages plus $15,225 Social Security, counted in full for MAGI) sits at 2.05x the 2-person FPL, far above the 138% FPL expansion ceiling. The only route left for a 65+ adult is the non-MAGI aged/blind/disabled pathway, which is not conferred by age: it requires countable income at or below Virginia's SSI-related ABD standard (roughly 80% FPL, about $17,300 for a couple) with a $3,000 couple resource limit, and $44,289 clears that standard by more than 2.5x even after the $20 general and $65-plus-half earned disregards (countable about $2,427/month). The spouse also received $0 SSI, so the SSI-recipient pathway never triggers, leaving medicaid_category = NONE. Every wrong model treated age 65+ as itself creating an aged pathway, or assumed the spouse's own $0 earnings rather than the couple's combined countable income governs that pathway's income test.

PolicyEngine's Medicare eligibility variable applies the standard age criterion, which both spouses satisfy because they are 71 and 69. The spouse's eligibility therefore equals Yes without requiring a separately listed work-credit history.

Virginia gives each taxpayer age 65 or older a $12,000 age deduction under Va. Code § 58.1-322.02(10)-(11), reduced dollar-for-dollar only when adjusted federal AGI — a measure that excludes taxable Social Security — exceeds $75,000 on a joint return. Virginia also subtracts the federally taxable Social Security ($2,338.25 of the $15,225), so Virginia AGI is $29,064 and AFYA is $29,064, far below the $75,000 joint threshold; both spouses therefore take the full $12,000, and $24,000 of age deductions alone wipes out Virginia AGI before the joint standard deduction and the $930 personal plus $800 age exemptions are even applied. Taxable income is $0 and the tax is $0 at any 2026 standard-deduction level. Every wrong answer either replaced the $12,000-per-person age deduction with Virginia's small $800 additional 65+ exemption, granted it to only one spouse, or left taxable Social Security inside Virginia AGI.

The correct 2026 AGI is $23,130: pension $18,340 + interest $400 + $4,390 of taxable Social Security. The $24,000 disability benefits and $48,000 veterans benefits are excluded from gross income, so provisional income is $18,740 + half of $44,080 = $40,780, which sits between the MFJ $32,000 and $44,000 thresholds and therefore includes only 50% × ($40,780 − $32,000) = $4,390 of benefits. That AGI is below the 2026 MFJ standard deduction alone ($32,200 base + two $1,650 age-65 additions = $35,500), and further below it once the $6,000-per-senior deduction ($12,000) is applied, so taxable income and tax before refundable credits are $0, and NIIT is $0 because AGI is far under $250,000. Nine models manufactured taxable income by pulling the non-taxable disability benefits into gross/provisional income (which also flips Social Security from the 50% tier to the 85% tier), by taxing 100% of Social Security, or by filing the couple as a single individual. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 0.00; the alternative is 1,890.30. The prompt lists disability benefits from employment without saying who paid for the coverage. Benefits from employer-paid coverage are included in gross income (26 U.S.C. 105(a)); benefits from coverage the employee paid for with after-tax money are excluded (26 U.S.C. 104(a)(3)). The reference excludes them; the alternative value includes them. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (who paid for the coverage behind listed employment disability benefits, which decides whether they are taxable).

Employee payroll taxes apply to covered wages and other employment compensation, not Social Security retirement benefits, pensions, disability benefits, veterans benefits, or taxable interest. Because the household has no wages or other payroll-taxable earnings, every employee-side payroll-tax component is zero.

Medicaid eligibility for the spouse cannot be established by treating the spouse's lack of individually reported income as zero countable income. The spouse qualifies through no Washington Medicaid pathway: the engine assigns category NONE, records no SSI, and calculates household MAGI at 2.90 times FPL, above the applicable MAGI limits.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine deducts the $1,118 traditional IRA contribution above the line (above-the-line deductions of $2,699.98 = $1,582 capital loss + $1,118). It caps the deduction only by the age-based dollar limit and does not apply IRC §219(b)(1)(B), which limits the deduction to compensation includible in gross income. This household has $0 wages and $0 self-employment income, and neither spouse has compensation for a §219(c) spousal IRA, so the allowable deduction is $0 and tax is about $22,400.71.
case_annotation: The reference deducts the $1,118 traditional IRA contribution above the line, which brings AGI to $182,172.27. It then subtracts the $32,200 2026 MFJ standard deduction, taxes $146,212.27 of ordinary income at the OBBBA-indexed brackets (10% to $24,800, 12% to $100,800, then 22%), and taxes $3,760 of qualified dividends at 15%. The largest group of models ($22,400.71 / $22,401) followed the same path but disallowed the IRA deduction because the household has no compensation. That alone accounts for a gap of about $246 ($1,118 × 22%). Most other models made their own errors: some used pre-TCJA sunset law (personal exemptions and 15%/25% brackets) even though OBBBA made the TCJA rates and exemption repeal permanent; some used 2025 brackets or wrong standard deductions; some deducted 401(k) deferrals against non-wage income or excluded Social Security; and some submitted numbers that did not match their own calculations. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_model_issue_fixed; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 22,154.70; the corrected value is 22,400.65. PolicyEngine deducts traditional IRA contributions above the compensation limit and counts a dependent's contributions on the filers' return. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 219(a), 219(b)(1)(B), 219(c), 219(f)(1); IRS Notice 2025-67).

Medicare eligibility without disability or ESRD requires age 65. The head is 64 for the whole 2026 tax year, and the prompt says ages and statuses stay constant all year. The head is listed with no disability, no SSDI, and no ESRD, so no non-age pathway applies. Two models correctly reasoned "64 < 65, not eligible" but still submitted 1. The other two invented a "near-term" or "projected" eligibility rule that doesn't exist.

Usual weekly hours and employer-sponsored insurance establish work and coverage facts but do not supply wage income or an hourly rate. Because unlisted numeric inputs are zero, both people have zero wages subject to employee Social Security and Medicare taxes, so employee payroll tax is zero.

Texas imposes no state individual income tax, and exclusive Texas residency makes every other state's income-tax component zero. The aggregate state income tax before refundable credits is therefore the sum of 51 zero components, yielding $0.

The case turns on the IRC §86 provisional-income test: provisional income is $1,200 interest − $135 partnership loss + half of the $51,475 Social Security benefit = $26,802.50, which sits below the $32,000 MFJ base amount, so none of the Social Security enters gross income. AGI is therefore $1,065, far below the 2026 MFJ standard deduction, leaving $0 taxable income and $0 income tax before credits; the $1,200 of interest is nowhere near the $250,000 MFJ NIIT threshold, and the traditional 401(k)/IRA contributions are irrelevant because the household has no earned income to support them. Every wrong model produced a positive tax by pulling Social Security benefits into taxable income — fully, at 85%, or by keeping them in the AGI it then reduced by the standard deduction — except Sonnet, which reached $0 and then overrode it with imputed wages the facts do not list.

The head’s Medicaid MAGI is approximately $52,540, or 2.39 times FPL, because the income calculation includes the applicable Social Security retirement income rather than reducing MAGI to taxable interest less the partnership loss. At that income level the head qualifies through neither New York’s expansion-adult category nor any non-MAGI categorical pathway, so medicaid_category is NONE.

Medicare eligibility starts at age 65. Before 65, a person qualifies only after 24 months of Social Security disability benefits or because of ESRD/ALS. The head is 62, has no listed disability, and does not qualify through any of those routes. Taking reduced Social Security retirement benefits early at 62 does not make someone eligible for Medicare. Every wrong model either treated Social Security retirement income as a path to Medicare or misapplied the age-65 test.

Payroll tax applies to wages and other covered earned compensation, not Social Security retirement benefits, taxable interest, or partnership/S-corporation losses. Because unlisted wages and hourly rates are zero, the household has no employee payroll-tax base and employee payroll tax is $0.

New York's ACA expansion pathway requires the spouse's MAGI income level to be at or below 138% of FPL. The household's applicable MAGI is 2.39 times FPL, and the 51-year-old spouse has no disability, blindness, SSI, age-based, dependent, or other categorical pathway, so the Medicaid category is NONE.

Both spouses show 40-hour work weeks but no wage amount, and the prompt directs that unlisted numeric inputs be treated as 0, so the household's only non-Social-Security income is $1,200 of taxable interest less a $135 partnership loss = $1,065. Provisional income is $1,065 + half of $51,475 = $26,803, below the $32,000 married-filing-jointly base, so none of the Social Security benefit is federally taxable, and New York subtracts any taxable Social Security from federal AGI regardless. New York AGI of $1,065 is entirely absorbed by the ~$16,050 MFJ standard deduction, leaving $0 of NY taxable income and $0 of tax before refundable credits. Every wrong answer either taxed the $51,475 Social Security benefit, imputed phantom wages from the hours-worked fact, or both.

This couple has no wages or rent, so its federal AGI is only about $1,065: $1,200 of interest minus a $135 partnership loss. None of the $51,475 in Social Security is taxable, because provisional income is below the $32,000 joint base. The only NY credit this low income could trigger is the household credit under Tax Law §606(b), and that credit is nonrefundable. It can only reduce NY tax, which is already zero, and it never counts toward state_refundable_credits. None of New York's refundable credits apply either: there is no federal EITC, no qualifying child, and no property tax or rent for the real property tax credit, so the refundable total is $0.

PolicyEngine applies the 2026 rules under OBBBA, which made the TCJA rules permanent. AGI is $536,764.50: wages less traditional 401(k) deferrals, where each spouse's $27,240 traditional+Roth request is cut to the $24,500 combined limit, pro-rating traditional deferrals to $20,825 each ($41,650 total); plus the $2,164 IRA deduction, the $3,000 capital-loss deduction, and no taxable state refund. The household takes the $32,200 standard deduction plus the $1,070 non-itemizer cash charitable deduction, because the phased-down SALT cap (~$30.9k) and the charity gift, which the 0.5%-of-AGI floor wipes out, cannot beat it. Tax is $89,095.92 of ordinary bracket tax, plus 15% on $77,920 of qualified dividends ($11,688), plus 3.8% NIIT on $150,578.34. The wrong answers did one or more of these: applied TCJA-sunset law (pre-TCJA brackets, Pease, personal exemptions, AMT), invented mortgage interest from a balance with no interest given, left out NIIT, subtracted ESI premiums from wages, or, among the near-misses, missed the 401(k) pro-rating, the refund exclusion, and the non-itemizer charitable deduction. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 106,505.90; the corrected value is 107,198.34. PolicyEngine deducts traditional IRA contributions without the active-participant phase-out. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 219(g); IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 ranges)).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The federal parts were easy to get right: Social Security is 6.2% of $180,000 plus 6.2% of the $184,500 2026 cap on the spouse's $250,000, totaling $22,599. Medicare is 1.45% of $430,000, or $6,235. Additional Medicare Tax is 0.9% of the $180,000 above the $250,000 MFJ threshold, or $1,620. The trap that separated the answers is California SDI. In 2026 it is 1.3% of all gross wages with no wage ceiling, so it is $5,590 on $430,000. Most models left SDI out, used the old 1.1%/1.2% rates, applied the wage cap that was repealed in 2024, or subtracted employer-sponsored insurance (ESI) premiums from the payroll wage base, which the engine taxes in full.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

In the engine, the California itemized deduction is only the $17,280 real estate tax. California has no SALT cap. No mortgage interest is listed, so the $2.85M balance produces $0 of deduction. The $2,574 of charity is below the 0.5%-of-AGI floor on itemized charitable gifts, so it adds nothing, and unreimbursed employee expenses are not counted. The high-income limitation cuts the $17,280 by 6% of AGI above $504,411 ($1,941.21), leaving $15,338.79. That beats the $11,412 standard deduction and gives taxable income of $521,425.72. The 2026 joint rate schedule produces $41,208.45 of tax, and the partly phased-out exemption credits of $156.93 reduce it to $41,051.51. Most models deducted too much: they invented mortgage interest, added charity and employee expenses, skipped the 6% limitation, or subtracted insurance premiums and IRA contributions. Others added tax-exempt pension or interest income, used the standard deduction, misapplied the rate brackets, or ignored the exemption-credit phaseout. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 41,051.51; the corrected value is 40,920.40. PolicyEngine deducts traditional IRA contributions without the active-participant phase-out; PolicyEngine applies the federal charitable deduction floor and the suspension of miscellaneous deductions to California itemized deductions. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 219(g); IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 ranges); Cal. R&TC 17024.5 (conformity date), 17076).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The correct answer needs three things. First, taxable SSDI is $13,784.12: provisional income is $35,280 + $9,642.50 = $44,922.50, and the taxable amount is the lesser of 85% × $19,285 and 0.85 × ($44,922.50 − $34,000) + $4,500. The tax-exempt pension is not counted in provisional income. Second, the 2026 single standard deduction is $16,100, because OBBBA made the TCJA rules permanent, so there is no personal exemption. Third, the 2026 brackets are 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above that, which gives $1,240 + 12% × $20,564.12 = $3,707.70. The wrong answers fall into four groups: some applied the SS taxation formula incorrectly (taking the 85% cap instead of the lesser amount, using only the 50% tier, adding the $284, or treating SSDI as untaxed); some used stale 2024/2025 deductions and brackets; some assumed the TCJA had expired, with personal exemptions and a 15% bracket; and some submitted a value that differs from their own calculation. Developer adjudication (2026-09-29): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (taxable_income_or_deductions). The judge labeled seven models' rows reference_later_law because they applied the pre-TCJA rules scheduled to return in 2026 (a smaller standard deduction, a personal exemption and a 15% second bracket). The reference applies the permanent TCJA parameters of P.L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025, before the July 3, 2026 reference freeze, and the benchmark scores law published before the freeze; the rows are model errors.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The head is 56, so Medicare's age-65 test fails, and the only other route is disability entitlement. Under 42 U.S.C. 426(b), that route requires 24 months of SSDI entitlement, not just SSDI income in the current year. The household lists no disability status, no months of SSDI receipt, no ESRD and no ALS. The prompt says unlisted status inputs are false and unlisted numbers are 0, and a constant status across one tax year shows at most 12 months. All 22 models treated the $19,285 of SSDI income as proof of Medicare eligibility, either by assuming the 24-month wait was already met or by claiming PolicyEngine grants eligibility whenever SSDI is positive, so they answered Yes instead of No. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 0.0 to 1.0 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. In law the under-65 route needs 24 months of SSDI entitlement; a year-round recipient has at least 12. The facts do not settle it.

Payroll tax applies to wages and other FICA-covered earned compensation, not to Social Security disability benefits or private pension income. The prompt specifies no wage or self-employment income and requires unlisted numeric inputs to be zero, so the employee payroll-tax base is zero and payroll tax is $0.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Idaho starts from federal AGI of $49,064.12 and subtracts the $13,784.12 of federally taxable Social Security, leaving $35,280. The $16,100 standard deduction brings Idaho taxable income to $19,180. For 2026 Idaho taxes income at 5.3%, but the first $4,920 for a single filer is taxed at zero, so the tax is 0.053 × ($19,180 − $4,920) = $755.78. Most models got to $19,180 and then left out the zero-rate amount, used the old 5.695% or 5.8% rate, or used an out-of-date zero-rate amount. Others never subtracted Social Security, used the wrong standard deduction, or wrongly applied Idaho's retirement-benefits deduction to a private pension for someone aged 56. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (state_local_rule). The frozen reference is 755.78; the corrected value is 651.32. PolicyEngine omits Idaho's subtraction for health insurance premiums the taxpayer pays. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (Idaho Code 63-3022P; Idaho Form 39R).

The whole $155 is the Idaho Grocery Credit. It is fully refundable and has no income phase-out. It is reduced only for months when the person gets SNAP or is incarcerated, and this filer qualifies for all 12 months. Idaho's 2025 legislation (HB 231) raised the per-person amount for filers under 65 from $120 to $155 starting in tax year 2025. The wrong answers split into two groups. One group used outdated per-person amounts: $120 under 2023–2024 law, $100 under earlier law, or $140, which was the old age-65+ amount. The other group answered $0, treating the credit as nonrefundable, phased out by income, repealed, or nonexistent.

CHIP is a residual program: it covers children who do NOT qualify for Medicaid, so its income band has a floor at the state's children's Medicaid limit, not just a ~350% FPL ceiling. With household income of about $30,915 for a family of eight — roughly 54% of FPL — the 17-year-old clears New Jersey's Medicaid test in the OLDER_CHILD category, and that Medicaid eligibility forecloses CHIP. All nine models tested only the upper CHIP ceiling and read very low income as evidence for CHIP, when low income is exactly what routes the child to Medicaid instead.

A 17-year-old tax-unit dependent falls within New Jersey's OLDER_CHILD Medicaid category. The household's MAGI is 0.55 times FPL, below the category's income threshold, so the child is eligible without any additional eligibility trigger.

WIC child eligibility is restricted to infants and children younger than age five; a 17-year-old is categorically ineligible regardless of household income. Both models incorrectly treated age 17 as within the WIC child age range.

CHIP is residual coverage: Title XXI covers only targeted low-income children who are NOT eligible for Medicaid, so the binding step is the lower Medicaid children's threshold, not New Jersey's upper ~355% FPL FamilyCare CHIP ceiling. At ~$30,915 for a household of 8 (roughly 54% FPL), the 14-year-old clears New Jersey's Medicaid limit for children ages 6-18 and PolicyEngine assigns him the OLDER_CHILD Medicaid category, which screens him out of CHIP. Every wrong model tested only the upper CHIP income ceiling and stopped there, converting "income low enough for CHIP" into "CHIP eligible" when that same low income instead routes the child into Medicaid.

New Jersey's older-child Medicaid pathway covers the 14-year-old tax-unit dependent because household MAGI is 0.55 times FPL, below the applicable income threshold. Eligibility follows directly from the child's age category and MAGI; no separate disability, SSI, or explicit Medicaid-enrollment fact is required.

WIC child eligibility is limited to infants and children under age five; it does not extend to school-age children through age 18. Child 2 is age 14 and therefore fails the categorical age requirement before the income test can establish eligibility.

CHIP is a residual program: it covers only children who do NOT qualify for Medicaid, so child eligibility is a band with a Medicaid floor beneath the CHIP ceiling, not a single upper income test. At roughly $30,915 for a household of 8 (~56% FPL), child3 at age 12 falls under New Jersey's Medicaid threshold for the 6–18 age group and is Medicaid-eligible in the OLDER_CHILD category, which forecloses CHIP. Every wrong model tested only the CHIP ceiling (NJ FamilyCare's ~355% FPL child limit) and read "income far below the ceiling" as affirmative evidence of CHIP eligibility, when income that far below is precisely what routes the child into Medicaid instead. Several went further and used the household's poverty and receipt of housing assistance as supporting evidence for CHIP, inverting the direction of the rule.

New Jersey places the 12-year-old dependent in the OLDER_CHILD Medicaid category. Household MAGI is 0.55 times FPL, below the applicable income threshold, so the categorical and income tests produce eligibility.

WIC child eligibility is limited to children under age five and also requires satisfaction of the applicable income test. Child 3 is age 12 and the household's approximately $30,915 income exceeds the applicable 185% federal-poverty threshold, so both categorical age and income rules prevent eligibility.

CHIP is a residual program: a child qualifies only if they are NOT eligible for Medicaid, so the binding test is the lower Medicaid bound for the child's age band, not the upper CHIP ceiling. Child 4 is 10, placing them in the OLDER_CHILD (age 6-18) MAGI category, and household income of about $30,915 for a family of eight sits near 54% FPL, far below New Jersey's Medicaid limit for that band, so the engine returns is_medicaid_eligible = True (OLDER_CHILD) and is_chip_eligible = False. Every wrong model applied only the CHIP upper income ceiling (~355% FPL), observed income far below it, and concluded "eligible" — exactly backwards, since the further below that ceiling income sits, the more certainly the child lands in Medicaid instead of CHIP. The very low income the models cited as proof of CHIP eligibility is the fact that disqualifies them from it.

Head Start is for preschool-age children, and child 4 is age 10. The age restriction independently makes child 4 ineligible, so household income eligibility cannot produce a positive result for this child.
New Jersey's older-child Medicaid pathway applies to child4 at age 10. As a tax-unit dependent with household MAGI of 0.55 times FPL, child4 satisfies the category's income test and is eligible.

WIC child eligibility is limited to children under age five, so a 10-year-old is categorically ineligible. The household’s approximately $30,915 of income also exceeds the applicable WIC income ceiling in PolicyEngine’s computation, providing an independent income-based disqualification.

CHIP is residual coverage: a child who qualifies for Medicaid is barred from CHIP, so the binding step is the Medicaid screen, not the CHIP ceiling. Child5 is 5 years old, and household income of about $30,915 for an 8-person unit (~54-59% FPL) sits far below New Jersey's Medicaid threshold for the under-6 (YOUNG_CHILD) age band, so the child is Medicaid-eligible and therefore CHIP-ineligible. Every wrong model ran a single test — is income below NJ FamilyCare's ~355% FPL child limit — and answered yes, inverting the logic: the further below that ceiling the household sits, the more certainly Medicaid captures the child and forecloses CHIP. None applied the Medicaid-first crowd-out or the separate, lower under-6 Medicaid income band that the child's age triggers.

Early Head Start serves infants and toddlers under age 3, while Head Start is the distinct program for preschool-age children. Child 5 is age 5 and therefore fails the Early Head Start age requirement regardless of household income or housing-assistance receipt.

Every model rejected Child 5 on age alone, treating preschool Head Start as serving only 3- and 4-year-olds. Under 45 CFR 1302.12(b)(1) the range runs from age 3 up to the age of compulsory school attendance, which is 6 in New Jersey, and PolicyEngine's Head Start age window includes 5-year-olds. The age test is met. The child is also income-eligible, both categorically through the household's SNAP receipt and directly because household income of about $30.6K is well under the poverty-guideline threshold for a family of 8. So the answer is eligible. No model reached the income or categorical test, because each stopped at an age cutoff that was set too low.
A five-year-old in New Jersey falls within the YOUNG_CHILD Medicaid category. At MAGI equal to 0.55 times FPL, the child satisfies that category's income test and is Medicaid eligible.

WIC's child category covers children from age 1 up to their 5th birthday, so ages 1 through 4. A child whose age is listed as 5 has already turned 5 and has aged out. Income does not decide this case: the age-1 Child 6 is WIC-eligible in the same household, so the household meets the income test. All 13 models treated age 5 as still inside the WIC age window, reading 'under 5' or 'up to the 5th birthday' as if it included age 5.

CHIP is residual coverage: PolicyEngine returns is_chip_eligible False for any child who already qualifies for Medicaid. The 1-year-old in this eight-person New Jersey household, with income near $30,915 (roughly 54% FPL), falls squarely inside the YOUNG_CHILD Medicaid category, so the Medicaid flag is 1 and the CHIP flag is 0. All twelve models tested only the upper NJ FamilyCare CHIP ceiling (300–355% FPL), found the household far beneath it, and treated that as proof of CHIP eligibility — when clearing that ceiling by such a margin is exactly what places the child under the lower young-child Medicaid threshold. Several went further and merged Medicaid and CHIP into a single "NJ FamilyCare" eligibility, erasing the mutual exclusivity that decides this output.

Early Head Start serves infants and toddlers under age 3, so age 1 satisfies the program’s age requirement. The household’s approximately $30,915 annual income is below the applicable 100% federal poverty line for this eight-person household, making Child 6 eligible.

Head Start requires both preschool-age categorical eligibility and satisfaction of the program's income or another qualifying eligibility pathway. Child 6 is age 1 and therefore belongs in the Early Head Start age category, not the preschool-age Head Start category; the household also exceeds the applicable income cutoff.

New Jersey Medicaid applies a YOUNG_CHILD eligibility pathway to the 1-year-old dependent. At a MAGI income level of 0.55 times FPL, the child satisfies that category's income test and is eligible without any additional benchmark-triggering fact.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The reference has two parts. The first is the full 2026 three-or-more-child EITC maximum of $8,231, with no phase-out because AGI (about $30,632) is below the 2026 MFJ phase-out threshold. The second is a refundable CTC of 15% × (earned income − $2,500). Earned income here is $26,800 wages plus $4,000 SE income minus the $282.59 half-SE-tax deduction, or $30,517.41, so the refundable CTC is $4,202.61. Only five children count for the CTC because the 17-year-old is excluded. Five times the $1,700 refundable cap is not binding, tax liability is zero, and the AOTC is $0 because the household has no qualified expenses. Most models missed on at least one of these steps: they used the wrong EITC maximum or applied a phase-out that does not apply, used the expired pre-TCJA $3,000 ACTC threshold, used gross $30,800 or 0.9235×SE earned income, or added an AOTC with no expenses.

Free school meals do not require an explicitly listed direct-certification indicator in the household inputs. The household qualifies through both routes established by the computation: its school-meal income is 55% of the federal poverty guideline, below the 130% free-tier threshold, and all household members are SNAP-eligible, which supplies categorical eligibility.

New Jersey expanded Medicaid under the ACA. Any non-elderly adult with household MAGI at or below 138% FPL qualifies in the ADULT category, with no disability requirement. This household has 8 members. Its MAGI is about $30.8k: $26,800 in wages, plus $4,000 in self-employment income minus half of SE tax, plus $115 in interest. That works out to 0.55× FPL, well under the 138% limit, so the 42-year-old head is eligible. Every model answered No for one of three reasons: it assumed non-disabled adults are categorically excluded, it misjudged where the income falls against the threshold, or it made up an exclusion rule.

WIC categorical eligibility is determined person by person, not conferred on every household member by the presence of an eligible infant or young child. The 42-year-old Head is not pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding and is not an infant or child under age 5, so satisfying the household income limit does not make the Head eligible.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Federal employee FICA on the spouse's $26,800 of wages is $2,050.20: $1,661.60 of Social Security plus $388.60 of Medicare. The head's self-employment income is excluded. The models diverged on the New Jersey employee payroll component. The reference counts only NJ temporary disability insurance at the 2026 rate of 0.19% ($50.92) and family leave insurance at 0.23% ($61.64), for $112.56 and a total of $2,162.76. Most models either left out NJ entirely, used outdated TDI/FLI rates (0%, 0.09%, 0.23%/0.33%), or added a NJ UI/WF/SWF employee contribution (0.3825%–0.425%) that is not part of this payroll_tax measure. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (payroll_tax_base). The frozen reference is 2,162.76; the corrected value is 2,276.66. PolicyEngine leaves the New Jersey worker unemployment and workforce contributions out of employee payroll tax. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (N.J.S.A. 43:21-7(d)(1); NJDOL 2026 contribution rates).

Reduced-price eligibility is a mutually exclusive lower tier, not a generic indicator that income is below the 185% FPL ceiling. This household is at 55% of the federal poverty guideline and also meets categorical eligibility, so it receives the superior free-meals tier and reduced_price_school_meals_eligible equals 0.

Self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of the $4,000 net self-employment income: $4,000 × 0.9235 × 0.153 = $565.18. The deduction for one-half of self-employment tax is an income-tax deduction and does not reduce the self-employment tax liability itself.

New Jersey's broad-based categorical eligibility makes the household eligible, so the spouse's $69,500 in bank assets does not count. The benefit then follows from FY2026 parameters. Gross income of $2,576.25 minus the $299 standard deduction (6+ people) and the $513.33 earned income deduction gives $1,763.92, which rounds to $1,764. Thirty percent of that is $529.20, rounded up to $530, and the $1,789 maximum for eight people minus $530 gives $1,259 a month, or $15,108 a year. There is no shelter, utility, or medical deduction. Most wrong answers either used outdated or invented maximum allotments and standard deductions, or skipped the rounding of net income and the 30% contribution and landed at about $1,260 a month. The $0 answers wrongly applied an asset test or income test.

New Jersey adopted the ACA adult expansion, so a non-elderly adult 19-64 who is not a tax-unit dependent qualifies on the MAGI pathway at or below 138% FPL, with no categorical hook, no asset test, and no benefit-receipt disqualifier. The test compares household MAGI to the FPL for the full household size: roughly $30,900 of wages, self-employment income and interest against the eight-person FPL is 0.55 x FPL, less than half the 1.38 limit. Housing assistance is excluded from MAGI and the $69,500 in bank accounts is irrelevant because MAGI categories carry no resource test. Each wrong answer either skipped this income test entirely or overrode it with a disqualifier that does not exist.

Medicare eligibility here turns on a single age test: the person must be 65 or older, and the Spouse is 41. The trap is the `is_disabled` flag: every wrong model converted it into a disability-based Medicare pathway, but real-world under-65 Medicare entitlement runs through 24 months of SSDI cash benefits (or ESRD/ALS), none of which is present — the household reports no Social Security disability income, and the prompt directs that unlisted income and status inputs be treated as 0/false. A disability flag alone establishes neither SSDI entitlement nor the 24-month qualifying period, so it cannot produce Medicare eligibility for a 41-year-old.

WIC eligibility is person-specific: an adult must be pregnant, breastfeeding, or within the applicable postpartum period, while infants and children qualify only through their own age category. Low household income and the presence of a young child do not make the child's mother or caretaker independently eligible.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

New Jersey taxable income here is NJ gross income ($30,915 = wages + full $4,000 SE profit + $115 interest, with no half-SE-tax adjustment) minus exemptions only. The exemptions are $1,000 for each spouse, $1,500 for each of the 6 dependents, and a single $1,000 blind-or-disabled exemption for the spouse, who gets only one even though they are both blind and disabled. That leaves $18,915 × 1.4% = $264.81. Models mostly went wrong in four ways: they claimed separate blind and disabled exemptions, used the wrong exemption amounts, subtracted the $50 property-tax credit (it is refundable, so it doesn't belong in this output) or the 18%-of-rent deduction (not taken, because the household takes the credit), or treated OTC health expenses as a deductible medical expense. Others zeroed the tax using a standard deduction or filing-threshold rule that New Jersey doesn't have.

The reference adds three New Jersey credits. The first is a $3,292.40 NJ EITC, equal to 40% of the full $8,231 federal maximum for 3+ children; at about $30.5k of earned income, the couple has not reached the MFJ phase-out. The second is a $2,500 NJ child tax credit for the two children age 5 and under, using the schedule enacted June 30, 2026 and keyed to NJ taxable income (well under $30,000 after exemptions), not gross income. The third is a $50 property tax credit for the renter household. Correctly applying the older $1,000-per-child CTC schedule gives only $5,342.40, so even flawless pre-enactment knowledge misses by $500. Most models also made their own errors on top of this: they phased out the federal EITC too early, chose the CTC tier from gross income, used outdated EITC maximums, left out the $50 credit, or denied that NJ has refundable credits at all. Developer adjudication (2026-09-29): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_later_law; adjudicated llm_error (state_local_rule). The judge labeled the case, and the rows of claude-opus-5.5 and gpt-6.1-sol, reference_later_law because those models applied New Jersey's pre-2026 child tax credit schedule. The reference applies P.L.2026, c.26, approved June 30, 2026, before the July 3, 2026 reference freeze, and the benchmark scores law published before the freeze; the rows are model errors.

New Jersey's WorkFirst NJ TANF is not a residual top-up: it is gated on countable income falling below the family-size eligibility standard tied to the maximum grant (roughly $770/month for a household of eight) and on countable resources at or below the $2,000 limit. This household's $26,800 in wages plus $4,000 of self-employment income is about $2,576/month, which clears the standard by a wide margin even after New Jersey's 50% earned-income disregard, and the $69,500 bank balance independently fails the resource test. Six children plus a blind and disabled spouse make the household read as categorically needy, which is the trap; family size raises the grant schedule but nowhere near enough to admit income at this level. The grant is therefore $0.

AGI is $105,900. That is $60,000 of gross wages, plus $20,400 of taxable pension, plus $25,500 of taxable Social Security, which is the 85% cap because provisional income of $95,400 is far above $44,000. The answer depends on using the OBBBA-permanent TCJA parameters for 2026: a $32,200 MFJ standard deduction, a 10% bracket up to $24,800 and 12% above that. Taxable income of $73,700 then gives $2,480 + $5,868 = $8,348. Most models went wrong in one of three ways: they assumed TCJA expired (personal exemptions and a 15% bracket), they used inflation-projected pre-OBBBA figures ($30,000–$30,900 standard deduction, $23,850–$24,500 bracket), or they subtracted the ESI premium from wages, which are already given as gross W-2 income. Several models worked out $8,348 or close to it and then submitted an unrelated number.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Medicare eligibility requires age 65 or an applicable under-65 pathway such as qualifying disability, ESRD, or ALS. Both adults are 57, and the prompt makes every unlisted disability or health status false, so the listed Social Security retirement income cannot be reclassified as evidence of disability-based Medicare eligibility.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Employee payroll tax here is 6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare on the spouse's full $60,000 gross wages: $3,720 + $870 = $4,590. No Additional Medicare Tax applies, and NC has no mandatory employee state payroll tax. The household facts list no Section 125 cafeteria-plan salary reduction. The ESI premium field is a premium amount and not a payroll deduction, which is clear because the head has $8,089 of ESI premiums with no wages at all. Most models invented an unstated pre-tax exclusion and taxed $51,861 instead of $60,000. Two others used the wrong rates or added an amount with no basis.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Medicare eligibility is absent because the spouse is age 57, below the standard eligibility age of 65, and no alternative eligibility status was listed. The required binary encoding assigns 0 to “No” and 1 to “Yes,” so the spouse’s result is 0.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

North Carolina's tax starts from federal AGI of $105,900: $60,000 in gross wages, $20,400 of taxable pension and $25,500 of taxable Social Security. The listed employer-sponsored insurance premiums do not reduce wages. NC then subtracts the $25,500 of Social Security included in federal AGI and its fixed, non-indexed $25,500 MFJ standard deduction. That leaves $54,900, taxed at the 2026 flat rate of 3.99% for $2,190.51, with no nonrefundable credits. The wrong answers fall into four groups. One subtracted the $8,139 ESI premium from wages, giving $46,761 and $1,865.76. Another used an old rate (4.25% or 4.5%) or the wrong standard deduction. A third invented itemized mortgage interest or NC credits. The last computed $2,190 and then submitted a different number.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The household has $22,000 of income, about 83% of FPL for a family of 3 (about 68% for a family of 4). That is far below Mississippi's Medicaid limit for children aged 6-18, which is 133% FPL plus the 5-point disregard. The 10-year-old is therefore Medicaid-eligible in the OLDER_CHILD category. CHIP only covers children who do not qualify for Medicaid, so Medicaid eligibility rules out CHIP. Every model tested the child only against the higher CHIP income ceiling and answered Yes. None of them applied the rule that Medicaid eligibility comes first.

Head Start eligibility depends on age, and the deciding fact is that Child 1 is 10, well above the preschool range of 3 to 4. The household's income is below the poverty guideline and it gets SNAP, so it meets the income and categorical tests, but those don't matter once the child fails the age test. The model's reasoning identified the age bar and ended with 'value = 0', yet its recorded answer was Yes (1). The error is therefore a mismatch between the submitted value and the explanation, not a mistake in reasoning about the policy.

Mississippi evaluates a 10-year-old dependent through the Medicaid older-child MAGI category. Household MAGI is 0.81 times FPL, below the applicable eligibility threshold, so the category and income tests produce eligibility.

To get WIC, a person must fit a category: pregnant, postpartum or breastfeeding woman, infant, or child under 5. In federal rules, the child category ends at the 5th birthday. Child 1 is 10, so the child fails the categorical test no matter how low the household income is, which makes child1_wic_eligible No. Every wrong model let low income decide the answer, or used the wrong age cap, or wrote that the child failed but still submitted 1.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

This is a married couple filing jointly with one qualifying child (age 10) and $22,000 of earnings. That income is above the end of the one-child EITC phase-in and below the joint phase-out start, so the household gets the full 2026 one-child maximum of $4,427. Federal income tax is $0. Under the OBBBA-permanent CTC rules, the refundable ACTC is min($1,700 refundable cap, 15% × ($22,000 − $2,500) = $2,925) = $1,700, for a total of $6,127. Most wrong answers either used the 2025 EITC maximum ($4,328) or another un-indexed figure, or got the ACTC wrong in one of three ways: the TCJA-sunset $1,000 credit, the full $2,000/$2,200 credit treated as refundable, or $1,800. A few also miscounted children by including the pregnancy, or applied phase-outs that do not reach $22,000.

This three-person Mississippi household has $22,000 in wages, which is 81% of the federal poverty guideline. That is far below the 130% free-meal cutoff. The household also receives about $407.90 a month in SNAP, which makes the 10-year-old categorically eligible for free meals, and PolicyEngine treats a 10-year-old as enrolled in K-12. So the engine puts the household in the FREE tier. The wrong answers came from three different errors: one model never ran the income or SNAP test, one treated the child's school enrollment as an unlisted input set to false, and one wrongly claimed income was above 130% of the poverty guideline.

Mississippi Medicaid eligibility for a nondisabled 40-year-old adult requires qualification through a defined categorical pathway; income below 138% FPL does not independently establish eligibility. The head’s MAGI is 0.81 FPL, but the Medicaid category is NONE because the head satisfies none of Mississippi’s available pathways.

WIC categorical eligibility is determined person by person, not extended to every member of a household containing a pregnant participant. The pregnant spouse satisfies the categorical requirement, but the 40-year-old head is neither pregnant, postpartum, breastfeeding, an infant, nor a child under age five, so the head is not WIC-eligible despite household income below the limit.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Reduced-price eligibility is mutually exclusive with the superior free-meals tier in this output. At a school-meal FPG ratio of 0.81 and with categorical eligibility, the household is classified as FREE, so it receives no reduced-price support.

The SNAP unit has three people. Pregnancy does not add a member. Monthly net income is $1,833.33 − $209 standard deduction − $366.67 earned-income deduction = $1,258. Shelter cost is only the $450 rent. The $411 energy subsidy does not give this household, which has no elderly or disabled member, a standard utility allowance under the 2026 rules, so there is no excess shelter deduction because $450 is less than half of net income ($629). The benefit is $785 minus 30% of net income rounded up to $378, which is $407 a month or $4,884 a year. Most wrong answers either added a utility allowance triggered by the energy subsidy, counted the unborn child as a fourth member, used older FY2025 deduction and allotment amounts ($204/$768), or skipped SNAP's rounding rules ($407.70 instead of $407).

CHIP eligibility requires the person not already qualify for Medicaid. At age 18, the spouse is Medicaid-eligible under Mississippi's OLDER_CHILD category, so that Medicaid eligibility precludes CHIP regardless of pregnancy status or how far household income falls below a CHIP-related threshold.

Mississippi Medicaid applies an OLDER_CHILD eligibility pathway to the 18-year-old spouse. The spouse's MAGI of 0.67 times FPL is below the applicable income threshold, so this category produces eligibility despite the spouse not being a tax-unit dependent.

WIC covers pregnant individuals who satisfy the program's income test. The spouse is pregnant, and the household's approximately $22,000 annual income is below the applicable 185% federal-poverty income limit, so the spouse meets both categorical and financial eligibility requirements.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Mississippi taxable income for this married-joint household is $22,000 minus the $4,600 MFJ standard deduction, the $12,000 MFJ personal exemption, and the $1,500 exemption for the one dependent child, which leaves $3,900. Mississippi taxes the first $10,000 of taxable income at 0% and applies its flat rate (4.0% in 2026) only above $10,000, so the joint liability is $0. PolicyEngine's per-spouse allocation gives the head $118 (4% of $12,950 minus $10,000), but the unit-level result is $0. Four models computed the $3,900 base correctly and then taxed it from the first dollar. The rest also got the deductions or exemptions wrong, and one of them used another state's credit structure.

The trap is the Social Security provisional-income test: half of the $23,736 benefit ($11,868) plus the $6,720 pension, $16 of dividends and $72 of capital gain gives provisional income of $18,676, below the $25,000 first base amount for a single filer, so none of the Social Security is includible. AGI is therefore $6,808, which is under the single standard deduction before any age-65 additional amount or the OBBBA senior deduction is even reached, leaving taxable income and tax of $0. A second, independent guardrail is that federal income tax before refundable credits is floored at zero — nonrefundable credits can only zero out liability, never drive it negative.

The head is 80, so the 138% FPL MAGI adult expansion group (ages 19-64) is closed to them. The only route left is the aged/blind/disabled pathway, which counts Social Security in full. Social Security of $23,736 plus the $6,720 pension and $88 of investment income comes to about $30,544, or 1.91x FPL. That is far above the SSI benefit rate and the 100% FPL aged/disabled standard, and with SSI at 0 there is no SSI-linked eligibility either, so the engine returns category NONE. All three models answered Yes. One asserted eligibility without testing income, one excluded most of the Social Security, and one used AGI, which leaves out the nontaxable Social Security.

Starting in March 2026, Arizona's broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE) covers households with gross income up to 200% FPL. That limit is $2,608.33/month, rising to $2,660 from October. This household's gross income is $2,539.33/month (Social Security, pension and dividends), which is under that limit. BBCE treats both the asset test and the net income test as met, so the $58,700 in the bank and the $2,138 net income no longer disqualify it. The benefit formula ($298 minus 30% of net income) comes out below zero, but a categorically eligible one-person household still gets the $24 monthly minimum. That gives $24 × 10 months (March–December) = $240. Every model answered $0. They either applied the regular asset and net income tests, used Arizona's old 185% BBCE limit, or treated a negative benefit formula as ineligibility instead of applying the minimum benefit.

Arizona’s standard deduction eliminates the remaining taxable income after excluding Social Security, so applying the 2.5% rate directly to gross dividends and capital gains is incorrect. The resulting Arizona income tax before refundable credits is zero.

Arizona's Credit for Increased Excise Taxes (A.R.S. §43-1072.01) is refundable and pays $25 for the taxpayer plus $25 for each dependent, capped at $100. The single-filer limit is $12,500 of income. This person's federal AGI is $6,736 because none of the Social Security is taxable at their income level, so one $25 credit applies. They don't need earned income, dependents, tax liability, rent, or property tax to get it. Nearly every model missed this credit, ruled it out with made-up requirements, or misread the income test. One model counted age and disability exemptions as extra credit units.

The only taxable income is the spouse's $88,927.65 in wages, and AGI equals that full amount. Veterans benefits are excluded, and the listed ESI premium is not subtracted from the gross wage input. Under OBBBA's permanent 2026 parameters, the MFJ standard deduction of $32,200 leaves taxable income of $56,727.65. Tax is then 10% of the first $24,800 plus 12% of the remaining $31,927.65, which equals $6,311.32, and no nonrefundable credits apply because there are no dependents. Most models went wrong in one of four ways: they assumed the TCJA had sunset (bringing back personal exemptions and a 15% bracket), used stale 2025 deduction and bracket figures, subtracted the ESI premiums from wages, or did the math correctly and then submitted a different number.

Federal refundable credits are zero because this childless joint tax unit has income far above the EITC phase-out range and has no qualifying child for refundable CTC. No education, rebate, or refundable payroll-tax-credit facts create another refundable federal credit.

Medicaid eligibility for the head uses household tax-unit MAGI rather than only the head's earned income. The household's MAGI is approximately $183,584, or 4.11 times FPL, exceeding every applicable West Virginia Medicaid income limit, and the head has no alternative categorical pathway.

Only the spouse has wages, so the correct answer is the 7.65% employee FICA rate applied to her full $88,928 gross wages: $5,513.51 Social Security plus $1,289.45 Medicare, or $6,802.96. The facts do not say she pays premiums through a salary-reduction (Section 125) plan, so the $14,717 in employer-sponsored insurance premiums does not come out of the FICA wage base. Veterans benefits are not wages, and West Virginia has no employee state payroll tax. The largest group of wrong answers (7 models) assumed a cafeteria plan that the facts never mention and taxed only $74,211. Most of the rest applied 7.65% to $88,928 and then invented an extra tax, made an arithmetic slip, or submitted a number different from their own total.

West Virginia AGI is the spouse's $88,928 of wages. The veterans benefits are excluded, and the employer-sponsored insurance premium input does not reduce wages. WV has no standard deduction, so the only subtraction is two $2,000 personal exemptions, which leaves $84,927.65 of taxable income. The deciding step is the 2026 MFJ rate schedule. It is the 2025 schedule (2.22/2.96/3.33/4.44/4.82%) cut by another 5%, to about 2.11/2.81/3.16/4.22/4.58%, which yields $3,092.19 rather than $3,255 (2025 rates) or $3,460 (2024 rates). Many models also changed the base: they subtracted the $14,717 ESI premium to get $74,211, made up a standard deduction, or applied invented credits.

The correct calculation is short. Start with wages of $45,000 minus the $1,042 traditional 401(k) deferral, add $2,000 of interest, subtract the $3,000 capped capital loss and the $49 IRA deduction, and AGI is $42,909. Subtract the $16,100 single standard deduction for 2026 (OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent, so there is no personal exemption) to get taxable income of $26,809. Tax at 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above that is $1,240 + $1,729.13 = $2,969.13. No nonrefundable credits apply: there are no dependents, AGI is above the Saver's Credit limit, and the elderly/disabled credit is phased out. Most models got AGI right and then missed the answer in one of four ways: they used 2024 or 2025 standard deductions and bracket edges ($14,600, $15,000 or $15,750; $11,600, $11,925 or $12,150), assumed the TCJA had expired and applied a personal exemption with a 15% bracket, made up deductions such as mortgage interest or pre-tax health premiums, or made arithmetic and transcription errors after reaching about $2,969.

A single adult with no dependent children or qualifying education expenses receives neither the refundable Child Tax Credit nor the refundable American Opportunity Credit. At approximately $43,450 of income, the childless EITC is also zero, and all other evaluated refundable-credit components are zero, yielding total federal refundable credits of $0.

CHIP eligibility runs through categorical gates first: coverage is for children under 19 and, at state option, pregnant women, so a 36-year-old head never reaches the income test — PolicyEngine assigns chip_category = 3 (categorically ineligible) and is_chip_eligible = False. The ~$43,450 household income and Indiana's Hoosier Healthwise/CHIP income thresholds are irrelevant to a person who fails the age/pregnancy gate, and the separate Medicaid pathways also return NONE for a non-aged, childless adult at that income in a state whose adult expansion he clears on neither disability-SSI nor MAGI grounds. The single wrong answer stated this categorical rule correctly in prose and then emitted the opposite binary.

Disability alone does not establish Medicaid eligibility; the person must satisfy a specific Indiana eligibility pathway and its applicable requirements. The head falls into Medicaid category NONE, receives no SSI, is not a dependent, and has MAGI at 2.69 times FPL, so no MAGI, disability-related, or state-specific pathway confers eligibility.

A person under 65 becomes eligible for Medicare on disability grounds only after 24 months of entitlement to Social Security Disability Insurance, or through the ESRD or ALS pathways. Being disabled is not enough on its own. The head is 36, has no Social Security disability benefits, and has no ESRD or ALS status. That means they don't meet the age-65 test or any disability-entitlement pathway, so they are not Medicare eligible. All four models treated the bare 'is disabled' flag as automatic Medicare eligibility and skipped the SSDI-receipt requirement.

The prompt defined local_income_tax by listing only the NYC income tax, the Philadelphia wage tax, the Kansas City earnings tax and the St. Louis earnings tax. PolicyEngine's local_income_tax variable also includes Indiana county income tax, which applies in every Indiana county. No county was given, so PolicyEngine placed the household in Adams County and applied its 1.6% rate to Indiana AGI after the $1,000 personal exemption ($41,909.38 × 1.6% = $670.55). The prompt supports two readings: if the four-city list is exhaustive, the answer is $0; if the list is only examples and the variable carries Indiana county tax with a default county, the answer is $670.55. Every model chose the first reading, and a few also wrongly said Indiana has no local income tax at all. Developer adjudication (2026-10-09): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned prompt_ambiguity; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (state_local_rule). The prompt places the household in Indiana but states no county. Every Indiana county levies its own local income tax (IC 6-3.6), at rates that differ by county. policyengine-us 2.15.17 left county income tax out of local_income_tax, so the frozen reference was $0.00. From policyengine-us 2.23.1 (PolicyEngine/policyengine-us#9694, which standardized local income tax) the engine counts Indiana county income tax in local_income_tax, at the rate of the county it assigns a household with no stated county. The reference therefore depends on the household's county, which the prompt does not state. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (county of residence (Indiana county income tax)).

Employee FICA applies to the full $45,000 of gross wages: 6.2% Social Security ($2,790, well under the 2026 wage base) plus 1.45% Medicare ($652.50) gives $3,442.50. Indiana has no mandatory employee state payroll tax, and wages are far below the $200,000 Additional Medicare Tax threshold. The most common wrong move was shrinking the FICA base. Four models treated the listed $2,080 health insurance premiums as a Section 125 pre-tax salary reduction, and one subtracted the traditional 401(k) deferral, even though elective 401(k) deferrals stay subject to FICA. The rest reached or approached $3,442.50 and then broke the total with arithmetic slips or made-up add-ons.

Indiana's 2026 tax is its flat 2.95% rate applied to federal AGI minus a single $1,000 personal exemption. Federal AGI is $42,909: wages of $45,000, minus the $1,042 traditional 401(k), minus the $49 IRA deduction, plus $2,000 interest, minus the $3,000 capped capital loss. Workers' compensation is excluded. That gives $41,909 × 2.95% = $1,236. Most models missed for one of three reasons. Some used the wrong 2026 rate (3.0%, 3.05%, 2.85%, 2.9%, 2.97%, 3.025%). Some invented exemptions or deductions that do not exist: a disability exemption for a non-blind taxpayer under 65, a health-premium deduction, a child-support deduction, or a standard deduction. Others built AGI incorrectly, for example by deducting the full $4,510 loss, including workers' comp, or skipping the 401(k) exclusion.

The household reports $47,000 of deductible medical outlays — $26,000 of health insurance premiums excluding Medicare Part B, $20,000 of other medical expenses, and $1,000 of over-the-counter health expenses — against an AGI of $32,137.94 (wages of $34,638 less the $2,500 statutory cap on the student loan interest deduction). The main trap is the head's 'is disabled' flag. For SNAP, a household counts as elderly/disabled only if a member receives a disability-based benefit such as SSI or SSDI (7 CFR 271.2). Elderly/disabled status is what removes the excess shelter cap and allows the excess medical deduction. The head receives no such benefit, so the shelter deduction stays capped at $744 and no medical deduction applies. Net income is $2,120.25 − $290.72 earned-income deduction − $209 standard deduction − $744 capped shelter = $876.51, which gives $298 − $262.80 = $35.20/month for January–September and $48.18/month for October–December after the FY2027 uprating, or $461.34 for the year. Most models used an uncapped shelter deduction and got near-maximum benefits. The zero-benefit models missed California's broad-based categorical eligibility, which sets the gross income limit at 200% FPL; $2,120/month passes that limit. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 461.339722 to 3596.039795 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. SSI itself stays $0 under either reading (the head's countable income exceeds the federal benefit rate); SNAP moves because SSI-disabled status switches on the elderly-or-disabled SNAP rules. The 2026-09-22 audit recomputes the alternative as 3,576.00 with every publication convention and upstream fix (the frozen-engine value above was 3,596.04).

California AGI is $22,534.34: wages minus the $2,778 traditional 401(k) deferral, plus the $8,000 taxable 403(b) distribution, minus the $130 IRA deduction. The nonrefundable credits ($153 personal exemption credit plus the $60 renter's credit) total only $213, so $12.78 remains. Models missed this small positive amount in four main ways: they claimed the credits wiped out the tax, left out the 403(b) distribution, used projected 2026 or older-year parameters instead of the 2025 values, or dropped or invented a nonrefundable credit.

California's CalEITC covers childless filers aged 18 and over with earnings up to about $32k in 2026. It does not depend on qualifying for the federal EITC or having children, and it is refundable. In the phase-out range, the credit is computed on the greater of earned income ($17,442.65) or AGI ($22,534.34). This filer's AGI is higher because it includes $8,000 of taxable 403(b) distributions, minus the 401(k) deferral and IRA contribution, so the credit is computed on AGI and comes to $95.15. Models that answered $0 wrongly denied childless or non-federal-EITC eligibility, or thought the credit had already phased out. Models that answered higher amounts ran the phase-out on wages alone, guessed at the credit schedule, or added nonrefundable credits.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Most models missed for one of three reasons: they assumed the TCJA sunset (personal exemptions, a smaller standard deduction and a 15% bracket); they used 2025 or misestimated 2026 thresholds; or they reached about $7,031 and then submitted a different, unsupported final number.

The spouse's $62,725 of wages are the only FICA-covered earnings. They are taxed at 6.2% for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare, which gives $4,798.48 ($3,888.97 + $909.52). The head has no wages. The $32,200 pension is outside the FICA base. The head's ESI premium is not subtracted from the spouse's wages. Ohio has no employee state payroll tax, and Additional Medicare Tax does not apply. Several models got this computation right but submitted a different number. Others added Ohio income tax, subtracted the ESI premium, used the combined employer-plus-employee rate, or counted wages for the head.

The reference has four parts. First, Ohio AGI is federal AGI ($94,925.30) minus the unreimbursed medical care deduction. That deduction is $180.60: $6,500 of premiums plus $800 of other medical expenses, less the 7.5%-of-FAGI floor. The premiums count only above the floor because the head can get employer-paid coverage. Second, two $1,900 exemptions apply because Ohio MAGI is over $80,000. Third, the 2026 rate schedule adds a base amount of about $332 to 2.75% of income over $26,050. Fourth, the $200 retirement income credit applies for the $32,200 pension. The most common wrong answer, $1,589.56, gets the exemptions and the credit right but leaves out the $332 base amount and the medical deduction. Most other answers also use the wrong exemption amount, use the 3%+ brackets from before 2024, subtract a federal standard deduction, or add or drop credits.

NC Health Choice merged into NC Medicaid in 2023. North Carolina now covers school-age children up to 211% FPL, plus a 5% disregard, as Medicaid (Medicaid-expansion CHIP) under the OLDER_CHILD category, not as a separate CHIP program. PolicyEngine finds the 11-year-old Medicaid-eligible at this household income. Because CHIP covers only children who fail Medicaid, that Medicaid eligibility makes the child CHIP-ineligible. Every model that answered treated the 211% band as a separate CHIP program sitting above a lower Medicaid limit. Each one called the child CHIP-eligible instead of routing them to Medicaid first and excluding CHIP.

North Carolina folded NC Health Choice (separate CHIP) into Medicaid. Children ages 6–18 are now covered in the Medicaid older-child category up to 211% FPL, or 216% with the 5-percentage-point MAGI disregard. The household's MAGI is $85,209 in wages minus the $2,778 traditional 401(k) and $130 traditional IRA deductions, or $82,301. That is 2.13× the 2026 FPL for five people, which is under the limit, so the 11-year-old qualifies. Most models used the old 133%/138% FPL older-child Medicaid limit. Others overstated income by double-counting overtime or using gross wages, used the wrong poverty guideline, or wrongly treated employer-sponsored insurance as a Medicaid bar. That ESI bar applies only to CHIP, not to Medicaid.

Child 2 is 11. In the engine, North Carolina's Medicaid OLDER_CHILD category covers this child at the household's income, so the child is Medicaid-eligible. CHIP only covers children who do not qualify for Medicaid, which makes child2_chip_eligible = No. NC folded NC Health Choice into Medicaid, so the income band that the models called "CHIP, above Medicaid and up to 211-216% FPL" is Medicaid coverage for a school-age child. All four models that answered found income below the NC children's limit but assigned the child to CHIP instead of Medicaid, and never applied the rule that Medicaid eligibility excludes CHIP.

MAGI is the spouse's $85,209 in wages minus the traditional 401(k) and IRA deductions, about $82,300. Against the 2026 FPL for a household of five (about $38,700), that is 2.13 times FPL. NC Health Choice was folded into Medicaid in April 2023, so NC Medicaid now covers children ages 6–18 up to 211% FPL, or 216% after the 5-point MAGI disregard, and 2.13 falls under that limit. The models got this wrong in three main ways: they used the old 133% Medicaid line for ages 6–18 (when 133–211% went to separate CHIP), they compared against 210–211% without the 5-point disregard or measured income against an older, lower FPL, or they treated employer-sponsored insurance as a bar to Medicaid.

Every model placed 9-year-old Child 3 in a CHIP band that sits above Medicaid, using the old 133%-to-211% FPL NC Health Choice structure. North Carolina moved NC Health Choice into Medicaid in 2023, and PolicyEngine finds Child 3 Medicaid-eligible under the OLDER_CHILD category. A Medicaid-eligible child is excluded from CHIP by construction, so the answer is No however each model computed MAGI. The decisive step is the Medicaid-first ordering with North Carolina's older-child Medicaid limit, not any CHIP income ceiling.

NC Health Choice, the state's separate CHIP, was folded into Medicaid in April 2023. Since then, NC Medicaid covers children ages 6-18 up to 211% FPL, or about 216% with the 5% MAGI disregard. The household's MAGI is about $82,301: spouse wages of $85,209, which already include overtime, minus the $2,778 traditional 401(k) and $130 traditional IRA deductions. That is 2.13 times the 2026 FPL for five people, so Child 3 qualifies in the OLDER_CHILD category. Most models used the old 133%/138% limit and assumed incomes above it go to a separate CHIP. Others compared gross wages instead of MAGI, left out the disregard, used the wrong FPL, or wrongly treated employer coverage as a bar to Medicaid.

2026 law keeps the TCJA structure — personal exemptions repealed, a $32,200 MFJ standard deduction — and adds the deduction for qualified FLSA overtime premiums, so the $7,746.26 premium comes out of taxable income rather than being stacked onto wages that already include it, leaving $42,354.26 taxable and $4,586.51 of tentative tax. Oklahoma expanded Medicaid in 2021, so a 21-year-old non-dependent adult qualifies in the ACA adult group if MAGI is at or below 138% FPL. The $50,000 of financial assistance is a non-taxable transfer. It is not part of AGI or MAGI, so MAGI is only the $312 of taxable interest, about 0.02x FPL. The rest wrongly said Oklahoma never expanded Medicaid, required a disability, pregnancy or parent pathway, or applied asset limits.

The household lists no wages at all: its only income items are $312 of taxable interest and $50,000 of financial assistance, alongside assets and expenses. Employee Social Security and Medicare taxes attach exclusively to wages and salaries under FICA (IRC §3101, on "wages" as defined in §3121(a)); interest is unearned investment income and financial assistance is a non-employment transfer, and neither enters the FICA wage base. With a zero wage base, employee OASDI, employee HI, and Additional Medicare Tax are each $0, giving a household employee-side payroll tax of $0.

SNAP eligibility requires satisfying Oklahoma’s applicable resource test before the benefit formula is applied. This one-person household has $4,250 in bank assets and $50,735 in stock assets, so it fails the resource limit and receives no SNAP benefit regardless of its low interest income or the maximum allotment.

The only taxable income in this household is $312 of taxable interest; the $50,000 of "financial assistance" is a non-taxable transfer that never enters federal AGI, and Oklahoma's income tax starts from federal AGI, while the $4,250 bank balance and $50,735 of stock are assets that generate no income under the "treat any unlisted numeric input as 0" instruction. Against Oklahoma's single standard deduction plus the $1,000 personal exemption, $312 of interest leaves zero Oklahoma taxable income, so ok_income_tax_before_refundable_credits — and therefore the 51-jurisdiction sum — is $0. Every wrong answer is produced by the same step: adding the $50,000 financial assistance into Oklahoma AGI and then applying the graduated OK rate schedule to roughly $37,000–$43,000 of invented taxable income.

PolicyEngine counts gross income from the household's income sources, which here is only the $312 of taxable interest. The $50,000 of financial assistance is not counted, so this single 21-year-old filer with one exemption receives $40. Most models looked only at the EITC, saw no earned income, and stopped. A smaller group named the credit but added the $50,000 of financial assistance to gross income, which pushed the filer over the $20,000 limit.

The trap is the family-size count: comparing $30,000 against the one-person 185% FPL figure of roughly $29,000 flips the answer, which is exactly the shortcut the wrong answer took.

Every model that answered stopped at the federal income test or the categorical-eligibility check and never applied Minnesota's universal free-meals override.
