WIC eligibility is person-specific and requires the applicant to be pregnant, postpartum, breastfeeding, an infant, or a child under age five. A 50-year-old head with all relevant unlisted statuses set to false fails categorical eligibility regardless of household income or another household member's circumstances.

The reference adds Minnesota Paid Leave, which began January 1, 2026, to employee FICA ($1,798 Social Security plus $420.50 Medicare). The engine assumes the employer withholds the largest employee share it is allowed to: 0.44%, half of the 0.88% premium, on $29,000, which is $127.60. Minnesota lets the employer pay that share instead, and the prompt says nothing about this. So "mandatory employee state payroll tax" can mean (a) the employee's 0.44% share withheld, giving $2,346.10, or (b) nothing, because the employer is allowed to cover the whole premium, giving $2,218.50. Almost every model chose reading (b). The real errors are the few answers that are neither $2,218.50 nor $2,346.10: a wrong Paid Leave rate, invented rates or adjustments, an employer-share mix-up, and missing outputs. Developer adjudication (2026-10-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned prompt_ambiguity; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (state_local_rule). The frozen reference is 2,346.10; the alternative is 2,218.50. The prompt counts mandatory employee state payroll taxes; Minnesota Paid Leave contributions are the employer's, which may deduct the employee share from wages but need not (Minn. Stat. 268B.14, subds. 1, 3 and 5a), and policyengine-us 2.15.17 counts the largest share the employer may deduct ($127.60); read as the amount the law requires of the employee, $0, the output is employee federal payroll tax alone. Found in the 2026-10-05 audit of state payroll components (reference_audit/2026-10-05-payroll, program_classification.json). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (whether the employer deducts the employee share of a state paid-leave or disability premium that the law lets it deduct but does not require, which decides whether that share is a mandatory employee state payroll tax).

Minnesota has universal free school meals, so PolicyEngine gives every student the FREE tier whatever the family's income. Reduced-price eligibility is false only because the better free tier replaces it. Income is not the reason: the household sits at 1.56 of the poverty guideline, inside the 130-185% reduced-price band. Every model that answered placed income in the federal 130-185% band and stopped there. None applied Minnesota's universal free-meals rule, which moves the student out of the reduced-price tier.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

SNAP eligibility ends at the gross-income screen for this three-person Minnesota household: $29,000 of wages plus $13,664 of Social Security dependent benefits produces $42,664 of annual gross income, above the applicable limit. Take-up assumptions and benefit-allotment calculations do not create eligibility after that screen fails, so the annual benefit is $0.

CHIP eligibility requires the person to be ineligible for Medicaid, not merely under age 19 and below the CHIP income ceiling. The 18-year-old spouse qualifies for Minnesota Medicaid under the OLDER_CHILD category, so that Medicaid eligibility precludes CHIP eligibility without regard to whether household income is below the CHIP threshold.

The spouse is 18, and under Medicaid rules anyone under 19 falls in the child category, whether or not they are married or claimed as a dependent. PolicyEngine puts the spouse in the OLDER_CHILD category (ages 6-18). Minnesota's income limit for that category is well above the spouse's MAGI of 1.56x FPL, so the spouse is eligible. Nearly every wrong model treated the spouse as an adult and tested household MAGI against the 138% FPL expansion limit, a parent/caretaker limit or a disability/SSI pathway. None of those is the category that decides this case.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

WIC does not cover every low-income woman of childbearing age or every adult living with a child. An adult woman must be pregnant, breastfeeding, or within the applicable postpartum period; the spouse has none of these statuses because all unlisted statuses are false, so she fails categorical eligibility regardless of the income test.

Minnesota starts from federal AGI ($29,000 wages plus the $1,916 of Social Security made taxable by the §86 provisional-income formula = $30,916), then applies two Minnesota-specific subtractions the models ignored or undersized: the Minnesota Social Security benefit subtraction, which removes the entire $1,916 for a joint filer at this income (far below the phase-out range), and the Minnesota dependent exemption for Child 1 (roughly $5,300, indexed). That leaves $29,000 of Minnesota income against a 2026 joint standard deduction of roughly $30,700 plus the dependent exemption, so Minnesota taxable income is zero and tax before refundable credits is $0. Every wrong answer pairs a too-small joint standard deduction with a missing Social Security subtraction and a missing dependent exemption, manufacturing a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of phantom taxable income taxed at the 5.35% first-bracket rate.

Starting in 2023, Minnesota's EITC-linked Working Family Credit was replaced by the Child and Working Families Credit (CWFC), which is one combined refundable credit. A child under 18 generates the per-child child amount, which is inflation-indexed for 2026. The working-family part is only 4% of earnings, capped at the base amount, with extra amounts only for qualifying children aged 18 to 24. AGI of $30,916 is below the married-filing-jointly phase-out threshold, so the full $2,187.60 applies. The wrong answers fall into four groups: they missed the CWFC entirely ($0), stacked an old-style EITC-percentage WFC worth $1,000–$2,000 on top of the child credit, used the unindexed 2023 amounts ($1,750 + $350 = $2,100), or applied a phase-out that does not apply here.

AGI is $83,451.23: $79,000 wages + $775 interest + the $243 state tax refund + $16,320 taxable Social Security (85% cap) − $11,400 SE loss − $1,487 HSA. Under post-OBBBA 2026 law, deductions are $47,500: the $32,200 MFJ standard deduction, 2 × $1,650 aged additions, and the $6,000-per-senior deduction for both spouses. That leaves $35,951.23 of taxable income, taxed at 10% up to $24,800 and 12% above it, for $3,818.15. The models mostly went wrong in four ways. Many left out the $12,000 senior deduction. Others assumed TCJA had expired, bringing back personal exemptions and the 15% bracket. Some dropped the $243 refund. Others claimed deductions that don't apply here: auto-loan interest, overtime, or invented itemized deductions. Several also made arithmetic slips or reported numbers that don't match their own working. Developer adjudication (2026-09-29): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 3,818.15; the alternative is 3,788.99. The prompt lists state and local tax refund income without saying whether the refunded tax reduced federal tax in the year it was deducted; policyengine-us 2.15.17 counts the whole refund as income (policyengine-us#9422, fixing issue #9122), while under 26 U.S.C. 111(a) none of it is income if the household took no tax benefit from the deduction. Found in the 2026-09-29 engine upgrade (reference_audit/2026-09-28, cluster salt_refund_gross_income_9122). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (whether the prior-year deduction of the refunded state and local tax reduced federal tax (prior-year itemization, the income-versus-sales-tax election, SALT-cap headroom)).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

This is a simple calculation: employee FICA of 7.65% (6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare) on combined wages of $79,000 gives $6,043.50. Both spouses earn well under the Social Security wage base, the $250,000 joint Additional Medicare Tax threshold doesn't apply, South Dakota has no employee state payroll tax, and the negative self-employment income doesn't touch employee payroll tax. Almost every model either reached $6,043.50 and then submitted a different number (arbitrary rounding, an invented adjustment, or an unexplained replacement) or multiplied 7.65% × $79,000 wrong. One model gave no answer.

Self-employment tax is a nonnegative liability assessed only on positive net earnings from self-employment. The listed negative SSTB amount does not create a negative self-employment tax or refundable tax offset, so the self-employment tax base and liability are both zero.

The calculation is simple: $59,220 of taxable pension income, minus the 2026 OBBBA single standard deduction of $16,100, leaves $43,120 of taxable income. Under the 2026 single brackets, tax is 10% of the first $12,400 ($1,240) plus 12% of the remaining $30,720 ($3,686.40), for $4,926.40, with no nonrefundable credits. The models went wrong in three main ways. Some assumed the TCJA would expire in 2026 and used an $8,300 standard deduction, a personal exemption and a 15% bracket, even though OBBBA made the TCJA rate and deduction structure permanent. Others used stale 2024 or 2025 deductions and brackets. Several did the arithmetic correctly, got about $4,926, and then submitted a different number anyway. A few added deductions or credits the facts don't support: mortgage interest from a balance alone, the elderly credit for a 56-year-old, or medical costs below the 7.5% AGI floor.

New Jersey Medicaid requires both membership in a qualifying eligibility category and satisfaction of that category's financial rules. This 56-year-old has medicaid_category NONE, and MAGI income of 3.71 times FPL exceeds the limits for all applicable MAGI pathways; the listed expenses and assets do not create another pathway.

Taxable private pension income is not wages and is excluded from the employee Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax bases. With no wages or other earned income listed, every employee-side payroll-tax component is zero.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The head is 56 and not disabled, so New Jersey's pension exclusion (age 62+ or disabled only) does not apply and the full $59,220 is NJ gross income. The only subtraction is the $1,000 single personal exemption. No medical deduction survives: the $1,000 'health insurance premiums excluding Part B' is the total that already includes the $1,000 'other health insurance premiums', employer-sponsored premiums are not out-of-pocket deductible, and OTC items don't count, which leaves about $1,100 of qualifying expenses, below the 2% floor of $1,184.40. The tax on $58,220 is $280 + $262.50 + $175 + 5.525% × $18,220 = $1,724.16. The models fell into three groups: those that applied the age-62 pension exclusion, those that built a medical deduction by double-counting premiums or adding the $7,389 ESI premiums, and those that used invented brackets, standard deductions, or numbers that didn't follow from their own work.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The correct path starts with AGI of $41,539, which is wages minus the $386 traditional 401(k) and the $18 traditional IRA. The ESI premiums are not subtracted again. Taxable income then subtracts both the $16,100 2026 OBBBA standard deduction and the $9,629 qualified overtime deduction. The overtime deduction comes off below the line, so it does not lower AGI. That leaves $15,810 of taxable income, taxed at 10% on the first $12,400 and 12% on the rest, for $1,649.25. Most models missed the overtime deduction or assumed the TCJA sunset. Others subtracted ESI premiums from wages, used 2024/2025 brackets, or claimed a Saver's Credit, even though the $41,539 AGI is above the single filer's eligibility ceiling.

A 44-year-old single filer with no dependent children or qualifying education expenses and $41,943 of wages receives neither EITC nor refundable CTC. All other refundable federal credit components evaluated to zero, so federal refundable credits total $0.

North Carolina’s Medicaid expansion does not make every adult aged 19–64 eligible; the expansion pathway applies an income limit. At 2.60 times FPL, the head exceeds the applicable MAGI threshold and qualifies through no other Medicaid category, so the eligibility category is NONE.

The FICA base is the full $41,943 of gross wages, so 6.2% Social Security ($2,600.49) plus 1.45% Medicare ($608.18) gives $3,208.67. The household facts never say the $5,789 of employer-sponsored insurance premiums is paid through a Section 125 salary-reduction plan, and the prompt says unlisted status inputs are false. Even so, the largest group of models (eight) subtracted that amount from FICA wages and landed on $2,765.78. The other wrong answers started from the right 7.65% × gross-wages calculation and then broke it by changing the number arbitrarily, rounding loosely, giving a placeholder, or giving no answer at all.

North Carolina starts from federal AGI. AGI is gross wages of $41,943 minus the traditional 401(k) contribution ($386) and the traditional IRA deduction ($18), which gives $41,539.45. NC then subtracts its $12,750 single standard deduction and applies the flat 2026 rate of 3.99% to $28,789.45, for $1,148.70 with no nonrefundable credits. The most common mistake was subtracting the $5,789 employer-sponsored insurance premium from the listed gross wages, which gives an AGI of $35,750. Another group subtracted the $9,629 federal overtime-premium deduction, which comes off federal taxable income, not AGI, and so never reaches the NC base. Other models used the wrong rate (4–4.5% instead of 3.99%), used the wrong standard deduction ($10,750, $13,750, $15,400, $15,500 or $21,500), or made arbitrary final adjustments.

Under PolicyEngine, CHIP only covers children who do not qualify for Medicaid, so CHIP is mutually exclusive with Medicaid. Child 1 is 7, and household income is about $22,992, roughly 70–73% FPL for a family of 4. That is well within Louisiana's Medicaid limit for children aged 6–18, so the engine puts the child in the OLDER_CHILD Medicaid category, and that Medicaid eligibility sets is_chip_eligible to False. Every model that answered checked only whether income was below a CHIP ceiling and marked the child CHIP-eligible. None of them checked first whether the child already qualified for Medicaid.

Head Start for preschool-age children requires the child to fall within the program’s preschool age range; a seven-year-old does not satisfy that categorical requirement. Income eligibility cannot override the age restriction, so Child 1 is ineligible even under an income calculation that falls below a poverty guideline.

Louisiana evaluates a 7-year-old under the Medicaid older-child category. The household's MAGI is 0.66 times FPL, below that category's 2026 income limit, so the child qualifies; the listed assets do not alter this MAGI eligibility determination.
WIC child eligibility is limited to children under age five. Child 1 is age seven, so the child fails the categorical age requirement regardless of household income.

Under PolicyEngine's rules, CHIP and Medicaid don't overlap. CHIP covers only children who are not eligible for Medicaid. Household MAGI is about $23K for a family of four, roughly 70% of FPL. That is below Louisiana's Medicaid income limit for children aged 6–18, so Child 2 is Medicaid-eligible under the OLDER_CHILD category and therefore not CHIP-eligible. Every model compared income only to the upper CHIP ceiling and never checked whether the lower Medicaid pathway applied first.

Head Start preschool eligibility requires satisfying the program’s applicable age and income rules; a six-year-old is outside the ordinary preschool-age category, and no fact establishes an exception such as delayed kindergarten entry. The household contains four people, and PolicyEngine’s traced income test also does not place this child within the qualifying threshold, so low income alone cannot produce eligibility.

Louisiana evaluates the 6-year-old under the older-child Medicaid category using household MAGI relative to the applicable child income limit. The household's MAGI is 0.66 times FPL, so the child satisfies that category's income test; the listed assets do not disqualify a MAGI-category child.

WIC child eligibility ends at the child’s fifth birthday, so a six-year-old is categorically ineligible regardless of household income. All four models incorrectly treated age six as falling within the WIC child category; the models that also evaluated income therefore never reached the correct result because they first misapplied the age rule.

The requested amount cannot fall below zero: taxable income and income tax before credits are zero, and nonrefundable credits used are capped at the existing tax liability. Refundable credits are excluded from this output, so the resulting federal income tax before refundable credits is $0.

Earned income is $7,468 in wages plus $15,525 in self-employment income, minus half of the SE tax (about $1,097), which comes to about $21,896. That puts the couple filing jointly with two children on the 2026 EITC plateau: past the phase-in end of about $18,290 and below the joint phase-out start of about $31,000. So the EITC is the full 2026 maximum of $7,316. Under the OBBBA rules for 2026, the CTC is $2,200 per child and the refundable cap is $1,700 per child, so the refundable CTC is the smaller of $3,400 and 15% × (earned income − $2,500), which is $2,909.35. Models mostly missed in three ways: they used the wrong EITC maximum, they applied the pre-TCJA $1,000-per-child CTC with a $3,000 floor, or they mismeasured the ACTC's earned-income base, either by skipping the 15% limit or by calculating net SE earnings wrongly.

The household qualifies for the free tier through two independent routes: SNAP receipt confers categorical eligibility, and school-meal income is 70% of the federal poverty guideline, below the 130% cutoff. The two K–12 children therefore generate positive annual free-school-meal support, so the binary output is Yes.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Louisiana has run the ACA adult expansion since 2016, so a 25-year-old non-dependent adult who does not receive SSI falls in the MAGI-based ADULT category, which has a 138% FPL limit. The head's household MAGI is about $22,992 from $7,468 in wages plus $15,525 in self-employment income. For a household of four that is 0.66x FPL, far below 138%, so the head is eligible. All four models said the income was above the limit. None of them compared household MAGI to the poverty guideline for four people, and some confused the expansion limit with Louisiana's much lower pre-expansion parent limit.

WIC does not extend categorical eligibility to a parent or caretaker merely because children live in the household. The head is not specified as pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding, and the children are ages 7 and 6, above WIC's under-5 age limit, so income eligibility and adjunctive eligibility cannot make the head eligible.

The requested payroll-tax output includes only employee-side FICA on the head’s wage earnings; self-employment income belongs in the separate self-employment-tax output. PolicyEngine applies the underlying wage amount and component-level calculations to produce $462.98 of Social Security tax plus $108.28 of Medicare tax, totaling $571.26.

Reduced-price eligibility is a mutually exclusive lower tier, not a general test of whether income is below 185% of the federal poverty guideline. At 70% of the guideline, and with categorical eligibility, this household receives the superior free-meals tier, so reduced-price support is zero.

The calculation is a single step: net earnings from self-employment = $15,525 × 0.9235 = $14,337.34. That amount plus the $7,468 in wages is far below the Social Security wage base, so the full 15.3% rate applies and SE tax = $14,337.34 × 0.153 = $2,193.61. The deduction for half of SE tax lowers AGI only. It does not lower the SE tax base again, because the 92.35% factor already accounts for it. Most models used the right method but made arithmetic or transcription slips. One wrongly applied the half-SE-tax deduction a second time, and one gave no answer.

The calculation is simple. Monthly earned income is $1,916.04. Subtract the 20% earned income deduction ($383.21) and the FY2026 four-person standard deduction of $223, which leaves net income of $1,310. 30% of that is $393, and subtracting it from the FY2026 maximum allotment of $994 gives $601 a month, or $7,212 a year. There are no shelter, dependent care or medical deductions, because no rent or mortgage payment is listed and no member is elderly or disabled. Most wrong answers came from using stale or guessed parameters, such as the FY2025 values of $975 and $204, a $1,000–$1,050 allotment, or a $198–$217 standard deduction. Others invented deductions, made arithmetic slips, or wrongly found the household ineligible.

CHIP eligibility requires the person to be ineligible for Medicaid, not merely under age 19 and below the CHIP income ceiling. The spouse qualifies for Medicaid under Louisiana's OLDER_CHILD category, so Medicaid eligibility precludes CHIP eligibility without regard to whether other coverage was listed.

The trap is that the 18-year-old is labeled \"spouse,\" and all three models let that label override the age-based pathway: PolicyEngine assigns her the OLDER_CHILD medicaid_category, which covers ages 6-18 in Louisiana and does not require being a tax dependent or an unmarried child. The income test is not close either — household MAGI is 0.66 x FPL, below Louisiana's ~142% FPL older-child limit and below the 138% FPL adult expansion limit, so both the child pathway and the adult pathway the models invoked return eligible. Every wrong answer therefore combines a category error (adult instead of older child) with an unperformed or inverted FPL comparison, and one model additionally imported a nonexistent asset test into a MAGI category.

WIC income eligibility does not independently confer eligibility: a person must also be pregnant, breastfeeding, postpartum, an infant, or a child under age five. The spouse is 18, all unlisted statuses are false, and the only children are ages six and seven, so neither parenthood, childbearing age, nor low household income places the spouse in a WIC categorical group.

Louisiana's 2024 tax reform took effect in 2025. It replaced the graduated brackets and the old combined personal exemption–standard deduction ($9,000 MFJ, plus $1,000 per dependent) with a flat 3% rate and a $25,000 standard deduction for joint filers. Federal AGI is $21,896: $22,993 of wages and SE income minus the half-SE-tax deduction of about $1,097. That is below the $25,000 MFJ deduction, so Louisiana taxable income is zero and so is the tax. Most models used pre-reform exemptions and brackets (1.85%, 2%/4%) or applied only the $12,500 single-filer deduction to a joint return, which left positive taxable income. One model reached $0 in its reasoning but submitted a different number.

Louisiana's EITC equals 5% of the federal EITC and is refundable. In this case it is the only state refundable credit. The household files jointly with two qualifying children and has earned income of about $21,900 (wages of $7,468 plus net self-employment earnings after the SE-tax deduction). That puts it on the federal EITC plateau, well below the MFJ phase-out start of about $31k, so the federal credit is the 2026 two-child maximum of $7,316, and 5% of that is $365.80. Most wrong models said Louisiana has no refundable EITC, or that its EITC is nonrefundable. The rest used the right structure but the wrong federal maximum, the wrong state percentage (3.5% or 50%), or wrongly applied the phase-out.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine leaves the $25,950 of estate_income out of irs_gross_income, so it is missing from AGI and from the provisional income used for Social Security, but still counts it as qualified business income for the $3,319.81 §199A deduction; this conflicts with IRC §61(a)(15) and §662(a), which put estate distributions in gross income, and with §199A(c)(3)(A)(ii), which counts QBI only from items included in taxable income.
case_annotation: The reference files the Head as single, because a surviving spouse with no dependent child does not get qualifying-surviving-spouse status. It builds AGI of $32,699.07 without the $25,950 estate income, so under the single $25,000/$34,000 thresholds only $10,129.10 of Social Security is taxable. It then subtracts the $16,100 standard deduction and a $3,319.81 QBI deduction, which is capped at 20% of the $16,599.07 taxable income, and taxes the remaining $13,279.25 at 10%/12% for $1,345.51. Every model that answered except glm-5.3 put estate income into AGI, and that alone pushed taxable Social Security to the 85% cap. No model took the QBI deduction. About a third also used joint/QSS brackets with the $32,200 deduction, and others fell back to pre-TCJA sunset rates, outdated 2025 figures, or invented credits that wiped out the tax. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_model_issue_fixed; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 1,345.51; the corrected value is 8,596.03. PolicyEngine leaves estate income out of gross income while counting it as qualified business income. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 61(a)(14), 662(a), 199A(c)(3)(A)(ii)).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Every Virginia Medicaid pathway open to a 61-year-old is income-tested: the ACA expansion adult group caps MAGI at 138% FPL, and the SSI-linked aged/blind/disabled group sits far below that and keys off SSI receipt, which is $0 here. This head's Medicaid MAGI counts the full $36,105 Social Security benefit (untaxed portion included) plus $26,800 in IRA distributions, $2,030 in pension, and $25,950 in estate income, offset only by a $6,260 self-employment loss, landing at 368% FPL — 2.7x the expansion limit — so the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE. All three models either asserted without arithmetic that MAGI fell under 138% FPL or treated the "is disabled" flag as a categorical pass that skips the income test entirely. Disability and the expansion group's waived asset test change which income test applies, never whether one applies.

Before age 65, Medicare eligibility through disability requires 24 months of receiving Social Security Disability Insurance. Being flagged as disabled is not enough. PolicyEngine checks age ≥ 65, at least 24 months of SSDI receipt, or end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The head is 61, has no listed SSDI months (unlisted inputs count as 0), and has no ESRD. Their $36,105 of Social Security is retirement income, not disability benefits. Every model treated the disabled flag by itself as enough for Medicare, and that is why they answered 1 instead of 0.

Employee payroll tax applies to wage and salary income, not estate income, Social Security retirement benefits, IRA distributions, private pensions, or self-employment income. No wages were listed, and the prompt requires unlisted numeric inputs to be zero, so the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax bases are all zero.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Virginia AGI is $48,519.97: federal AGI of $79,209.22 minus the $30,689.25 of federally taxable Social Security. Because the head has no dependent, a surviving spouse files as single and gets the 2026 single standard deduction of $8,750 plus one $930 exemption. That leaves taxable income of $38,839.97, and the tax is $720 + 5.75% × $21,839.97 = $1,975.80. Most models made the Social Security subtraction correctly but missed on the deduction. Some used the old $8,500 or $8,000 amount, which gives $1,990 or $2,019. Others gave the surviving spouse the joint $17,000–$17,500 deduction, which gives about $1,473. A smaller group skipped the Social Security subtraction or invented age, disability or retirement exclusions that don't apply to a 61-year-old with no disability income.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Every model got the same AGI the engine used ($28,000 wages + $4,300 taxable Social Security = $32,300, since workers' compensation is excluded and provisional income of $40,600 falls in the 50% tier between the $32,000 and $44,000 MFJ thresholds) or missed it, and then lost the case on the deduction side. For tax year 2026 the TCJA structure is permanent: personal exemptions remain repealed, the MFJ standard deduction is $32,200, the aged additional standard deduction is $1,650 per 65+ spouse ($3,300), and the OBBBA senior deduction adds $6,000 per spouse aged 65+ ($12,000) for a total of $47,500 — well above the $32,300 AGI, so taxable income and tax are $0. Six of the nine models instead applied a TCJA-sunset 2026 with a ~$16,500–$20,000 standard deduction plus revived personal exemptions of ~$10,200–$10,600, a combination that leaves a small positive taxable income taxed at 10%. The two that used a post-OBBBA standard deduction still failed by inflating includible Social Security or by treating the senior deduction as a tax offset rather than a $6,000-per-spouse deduction.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Arizona Medicaid expansion does not cover the head through the ordinary adult MAGI pathway because the head is over 65, and the head qualifies through none of the aged, blind, or disabled pathways. At 2.46 times FPL, with no SSI, no disability, and no dependent status, the head has Medicaid category NONE and is ineligible.

Employee payroll tax here is simple FICA on each spouse's wages: 6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare on $20,000 and $8,000, which gives $1,530 + $612 = $2,142. Social Security benefits and workers' compensation are not wages for FICA. Arizona has no mandatory employee state payroll tax, and Additional Medicare Tax doesn't apply because combined wages are far below $250,000. Nearly every model worked out $2,142 in its own reasoning, then submitted a different number, so the miss came from the final answer contradicting the model's own correct work, not from a wrong rule.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The elderly or disabled household exception removes the SNAP gross-income test but does not establish eligibility; the household must still pass the net-income test after allowable deductions. This household's $56,400 annual income remains too high after the applicable deductions, so it receives no minimum allotment because minimum benefits apply only after eligibility is established.

The spouse is 69, so Arizona's expansion adult group (ages 19-64) does not apply. The only route left is the aged/blind/disabled category, which has an income limit of 100% FPL, and that test uses the married couple's combined income, not just the spouse's own. The couple has $28,000 in wages plus $25,200 in Social Security, about $53,200 in total. That puts them at 2.46x the two-person FPL, far above the limit, so the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE. Every model treated disability or age as close to automatic eligibility, looked at the spouse's income alone, or ignored the income and asset limits it had just named.

Medicare eligibility applies at age 65, so the 69-year-old spouse qualifies through the age pathway without needing disability-based eligibility or 24 months of SSDI receipt. The spouse’s workers’ compensation and disability facts do not alter that age-based result.

The case turns on two Arizona-specific rules: Arizona subtracts from federal AGI all Social Security benefits included there, and Arizona's standard deduction conforms to the base federal married-filing-jointly amount (about $32,200 for 2026) with no additional age-65 amount. Removing the $4,300 of taxable Social Security leaves $28,000 of wages as Arizona AGI, which is more than $4,000 below the standard deduction, so taxable income is zero and the 2.5% flat tax yields nothing before refundable credits; itemizing is worse at $16,324 of mortgage interest plus real estate taxes. The wrong answers all manufacture a positive base either by shrinking the deduction — inventing $20,000, $22,000, or an unstated ~$22,700 figure, in two cases by grafting a federal-style age-65 add-on Arizona does not have — or by leaving Social Security in the Arizona base. One model produced the zero result and then overrode it, and one returned nothing at all.

Arizona’s refundable credits are not awarded merely because a married filer is elderly and has income below a general threshold. case_annotation: The reference gets Wisconsin AGI of $29,981.71 by subtracting only the $13,655.95 of taxable Social Security from a federal AGI that contains none of the $3,753 in capital gains, and it applies no retirement-income subtraction and no 30% capital-gain subtraction. It then takes the single sliding-scale standard deduction ($12,671.36) and $950 of exemptions, taxes $16,360.34 at 3.5%/4.4% to get $584.74, and subtracts the $300 school property tax credit (12% of the first $2,500 of property tax). The wrong answers fall into three groups. Models that applied the $24,000 age-67+ retirement exclusion got $0. Models that kept the $3,753 of gains (less the 30% long-term exclusion) and otherwise followed the same steps got about $415–$430. The rest misapplied the standard deduction, filing status, exemptions, rates, or the $300 credit (skipping it, overstating it, or inventing other credits). Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_model_issue_fixed; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (state_local_rule). Stat. 71.05(6)(b)9; 26 U.S.C. 852(b)(3)(B); 2025 Wisconsin Schedule SB instructions, line 5).

Federal FICA on $4,088 is $312.74 ($253.47 Social Security plus $59.28 Medicare). The rest of the reference is Colorado's FAMLI employee premium: 0.44% (half of the 0.88% 2026 premium) × $4,088.15 = $17.99, for a total of $330.73. The prompt asks for 'mandatory employee state payroll taxes', and it can be read two ways. Under one reading, the FAMLI employee share counts because the law lets the employer withhold it from wages, which is how PolicyEngine treats it. Under the other, it is excluded because Colorado lets the employer pay that share instead, and the prompt never says which the employer does. Almost every model chose the second reading and landed on about $312.73. The few others made genuine errors: a wrong FAMLI rate, an arithmetic slip, or wrongly cutting FICA wages by health premiums. Developer adjudication (2026-10-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned prompt_ambiguity; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (state_local_rule). The frozen reference is 330.73; the alternative is 312.74. The prompt counts mandatory employee state payroll taxes; Colorado FAMLI contributions are the employer's, which may deduct the employee share from wages but need not (C.R.S. 8-13.3-507(2) and (5); 7 CCR 1107-1 s. 1.4(6)(A)), and policyengine-us 2.15.17 counts the largest share the employer may deduct ($17.99); read as the amount the law requires of the employee, $0, the output is employee federal payroll tax alone. Found in the 2026-10-05 audit of state payroll components (reference_audit/2026-10-05-payroll, program_classification.json). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (whether the employer deducts the employee share of a state paid-leave or disability premium that the law lets it deduct but does not require, which decides whether that share is a mandatory employee state payroll tax).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Colorado's refundable credits available to this filer depend on two things. The TABOR surplus mechanisms (the sales tax refund and the senior housing credit) pay only when the state has excess revenue. The Colorado EITC is a percentage of the federal EITC. Forecasts showed FY2025-26 below the Referendum C cap, so no TABOR-funded refund exists for tax year 2026. The head is 66, above the federal childless-EITC age ceiling of 64, so there is no federal EITC for Colorado to match. The correct calculation is simple. AGI equals the full $36,275.59 in gross wages. Subtract the post-OBBBA 2026 single standard deduction of $16,100 to get taxable income of $20,175.59. The models failed in four main ways: (1) they subtracted the $21,208 employer-sponsored insurance premiums from the gross wages; (2) they assumed the TCJA expired, bringing back personal exemptions and the 15% bracket, even though OBBBA made TCJA permanent; (3) they used outdated 2024/2025 standard deductions and bracket thresholds; or (4) they correctly calculated about $2,173 but then submitted an unrelated number, or reduced the tax to zero with credits that don't exist or with the refundable EITC.

The eighth model used the correct $36,276, reached the correct disqualification, and then submitted the opposite value. That single $21,208 subtraction is what flips a 227% FPL household into a 94% FPL household and is the entire source of the wrong answers.

Michigan counts child support paid in gross income and deducts it only when computing net income (7 CFR 273.9(d)(5)). That leaves gross income at the full $3,022.97 a month, about 232% of the guideline, which fails both limits, so SNAP is $0 for the year. The wrong answers came from three errors: taking child support or health premiums out of gross income, still paying a benefit after finding the household over the limit, and a submitted value that contradicts the model's own finding that the household is ineligible.

Michigan's tax is a flat 4.25% applied to federal AGI ($36,275.59, the full wage amount; the stated employer-sponsored insurance premiums are not subtracted again) minus the 2026 personal exemption of $5,900. That gives $30,375.59 × 0.0425 = $1,290.96, with no nonrefundable credits. Most wrong answers came from projecting the exemption from memory ($5,000, $5,200, $5,600, $5,800, $6,000 or $6,200) instead of using $5,900. The whole $760.79 is Michigan's refundable Homestead Property Tax Credit for a renter, with no state EITC. The correct steps are: count 23% of the $10,560 rent as property tax ($2,428.80). Subtract 3.2% of total household resources, which equal the full $36,275.59 in wages, giving $1,160.82 and a remainder of $1,267.98. Then apply the 60% non-senior rate to get $760.79. Most wrong answers left out the renter credit entirely and only looked at the zero Michigan EITC. The rest changed one input of the formula: they used 20% (or 17%) of rent instead of 23%, a 3.5% threshold instead of 3.2%, or a different credit rate. Others subtracted the $21,208 employer insurance premiums or the $5,200 child support from household resources, or added a federal EITC that a childless filer at $36k cannot get.

That MAGI is the full $92,003 of wages plus interest, which is about 280% FPL. The $14,839 FLSA overtime premium is already inside the $92,000 of wages. Once the overtime premium is subtracted from MAGI, income falls into the CHIP band. Kept in, income is above Oklahoma's CHIP ceiling for a 9-year-old, and child2 is ineligible because Medicaid is also unavailable.

Child 2 has no qualifying Medicaid category, receives no SSI, and the household's MAGI income of 2.79 times FPL exceeds every applicable child Medicaid threshold, so eligibility is No.

Under OBBBA rules for 2026, the household's $92,003 AGI is reduced by the $32,200 MFJ standard deduction and by the qualified overtime deduction of $14,838.71. Most wrong answers omitted the overtime deduction, applied pre-TCJA or 2025 parameters, double-counted premiums to justify itemizing, invented AOTC, or mishandled the nonrefundable CTC.

The American Opportunity Credit needs qualified tuition and related expenses, and none are listed, so both its nonrefundable and refundable parts are $0. The $4,400 CTC (2 x $2,200) is fully used against tax owed before credits. Even after the $32,200 standard deduction and the $14,839 overtime deduction, that tax is about $4,900, and the refundable CTC only pays back CTC left over after tax, so it is $0. The reference rests on a 2026 Louisiana standard deduction of $12,835, which policyengine-us computed from published CPI-U under R.S. 47:294(B) but which no Louisiana publication stated before the 2026-07-03 freeze; Louisiana's first 2026 return amount, $12,838, came in Revenue Information Bulletin 26-019 on 2026-09-28. Excluded under decision d994, which keeps the published-amounts convention for every other reference (reference_audit/2026-10-05-louisiana). Reference depends on law published after the reference freeze; output excluded from scoring (Louisiana Department of Revenue, Revenue Information Bulletin 26-019, dated 2026-09-28: Louisiana's 2026 standard deduction is $12,838 for single and separate filers and $25,676 for the other statuses, the first 2026 return amount Louisiana published).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine deducts the head's $43.28 traditional IRA contribution above the line, which is the amount beyond the $3,000 capital-loss ALD in its $3,043.28 total, without applying the IRC §219(g) active-participant phase-out. The head's 401(k) elective deferrals make them an active participant, and joint MAGI of about $505k is far above the 2026 MFJ phase-out range ($129,000–$149,000), so the statutory deduction is $0 and the statutory liability is $104,225.30, $13.89 above the reference.
case_annotation: The reference applies the permanent 2026 OBBBA joint-filer parameters to taxable income of $472,578.56: a $32,200 standard deduction, no personal exemptions, and a 32% bracket running from $403,550 to $512,450. The only reductions are the $926.16 401(k) deferral, the $3,000 capital-loss limit, and the $43.28 traditional IRA contribution; ESI premiums do not reduce wages and Additional Medicare Tax is excluded. The total is $103,865.78 of ordinary tax, plus $127.20 on the $848 of qualified dividends at 15%, plus $218.42 of NIIT on $5,748 (interest plus dividends, net of the $3,000 allowable loss). Most models missed because they used the expired pre-TCJA schedule with personal exemptions, subtracted the $16,208 ESI premiums from wages, used the wrong standard deduction or brackets, left out or overstated NIIT, or added the $2,250 Additional Medicare Tax. The closest models differ only because they disallowed the $43.28 IRA deduction. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 104,211.41; the corrected value is 104,225.26. PolicyEngine deducts traditional IRA contributions without the active-participant phase-out. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 219(g); IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 ranges)).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Standard Medicare eligibility requires age 65 unless a separate qualifying pathway, such as disability or end-stage renal disease, applies. The head is 59 and all unlisted disability and health-status facts are false, so no Medicare eligibility pathway applies.

Only the head earns wages. The reference applies three components to the full $500,000: 6.2% Social Security on the 2026 wage base of $184,500 ($11,439), 1.45% Medicare on all $500,000 ($7,250), and 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above the $250,000 married-filing-jointly threshold ($2,250), for $20,939. Two errors account for most misses. Some models used an outdated or guessed Social Security wage base, such as $168,600, $176,100 or about $180,000. Others shrank Medicare wages by subtracting the employer-sponsored insurance premium or the traditional 401(k) deferral, even though the facts never describe a cafeteria plan and 401(k) deferrals stay subject to FICA. Other models used the $200,000 single threshold, made arithmetic slips, or submitted numbers that did not match their own work.

Medicare eligibility requires age 65 or an applicable disability or other qualifying pathway. The 55-year-old spouse has no listed disability or other Medicare-qualifying status, so the spouse is not eligible.

The OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent, so 2026 law uses a $16,100 single standard deduction, no personal exemption, and brackets of 10% up to $12,400, 12% up to $50,400, and 22% above that. The household's gross wages are AGI because the employer-insurance premium input does not reduce them, and the OBBBA auto-loan-interest deduction does not apply because no qualifying new-vehicle facts are given. That leaves taxable income of $50,868.68 and tax of $1,240 + $4,560 + 22% × $468.68 = $5,903.11. The models went wrong in three main ways. Some assumed the TCJA would sunset and restored the personal exemption and the 15%/25% brackets. Some used 2023–2025 or guessed 2026 amounts for the deduction and bracket thresholds. Others took $3,389 of ESI premiums (or the $950 of auto loan interest) off AGI. A few computed roughly the right figure and then submitted a different number.

A single 25-year-old filer with no children and $66,969 of wages receives neither a refundable Child Tax Credit nor an Earned Income Tax Credit in 2026. With the other enumerated refundable-credit components also equal to zero, federal refundable credits total $0.

PolicyEngine applies the employee FICA rates to the full $66,969 of gross wages: 6.2% Social Security ($4,152.06) plus 1.45% Medicare ($971.05) equals $5,123.10. The listed employer-sponsored insurance premium ($3,389) does not reduce the payroll-tax wage base. The household facts never say the premium is paid through a Section 125 cafeteria plan, and the prompt forbids inferring unlisted facts. Eight models subtracted the premium anyway and taxed $63,580, which gives $4,863.87. The two GPT-5.4 models used the correct base and rates but multiplied them out wrong.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Idaho taxable income here is federal AGI of $66,968.68 (wages are not reduced by the ESI premium) minus the $16,100 standard deduction, which gives $50,868.68. Idaho's 2026 schedule taxes the first $4,920 of a single filer's taxable income at 0% and everything above it at a flat 5.3%: 5.3% × $45,948.68 = $2,435.28, and no nonrefundable credits apply. Most models left out the indexed zero bracket, which pushes them to about $2,696. Others used the old 5.695%/5.8% rates or progressive brackets, used an outdated standard deduction ($15,000, $15,750 or $8,300), or subtracted the $3,389 ESI premium from AGI. The closest answers missed only because they used the 2025 or a misestimated zero-bracket amount instead of $4,920. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (state_local_rule). The frozen reference is 2,435.28; the corrected value is 2,176.06. PolicyEngine omits Idaho's subtraction for health insurance premiums the taxpayer pays. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (Idaho Code 63-3022P; Idaho Form 39R).

Idaho's grocery credit is a refundable per-person income tax credit with no income limit or phase-out. For 2026, after the 2025 increase (HB 231), the amount is $155 for a resident under 65. This full-year, 25-year-old resident who received no SNAP qualifies for all 12 months, so state refundable credits equal $155. About half the models said $0, either calling the credit nonrefundable or inventing an income limit. Most of the rest knew it was refundable but used an older amount: $100, $120, or $150.

CHIP eligibility requires the child to be ineligible for Medicaid; satisfying a CHIP income ceiling alone is not sufficient. At this very low household income, the 10-year-old qualifies for Medicaid under North Carolina’s OLDER_CHILD category, and that Medicaid eligibility excludes the child from CHIP.

Child 1 qualifies through the ordinary children's MAGI pathway: at age 10 he falls in the OLDER_CHILD category (ages 6–18), whose North Carolina income limit is 133% FPL plus the 5-percentage-point disregard, and NC folded its separate NC Health Choice tier into Medicaid so school-age children are covered under Medicaid rather than being pushed to CHIP. The household's only income is $17,100 of self-employment earnings, which after the deductible half of SE tax leaves MAGI at 0.58 × FPL for a family of three — a fraction of the applicable limit. Both models returned 0 without ever performing that categorical-plus-income test: one asserted an income failure that the arithmetic contradicts, the other treated unlisted household facts as missing prerequisites even though the prompt instructs that unlisted booleans are false and take-up is assumed.

WIC categorical eligibility covers pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women, infants, and children under age five; it does not extend to nutritionally at-risk school-age children. Child 1 is age 10, so income eligibility and another household member’s WIC receipt cannot make Child 1 eligible.

The decisive CHIP rule is categorical: a child who qualifies for Medicaid cannot also qualify for CHIP. Child 2 qualifies for Medicaid in the young-child category, so the CHIP income ceiling and employer-sponsored insurance do not alter the result.

Early Head Start serves children from birth to age 3 in households at or below 100% of the federal poverty line, and Child 2 at age 2 clears the age band while the household clears the income test. The income trap is that the only earnings listed, $17,100 of "sstb self employment income before lsr," is a QBI-classification input that does not feed self-employment income, leaving countable household income at $0 — and even taken at face value, $17,100 is below 100% FPL for a three-person household. Both wrong answers denied eligibility: one by treating that phantom income plus a nonexistent asset test as disqualifying, the other by reversing the under-3 age comparison.

Preschool Head Start serves children from age 3 until they reach kindergarten age. Infants and toddlers under 3 fall under Early Head Start. Child 2 is 2, so the age test fails no matter how low the household income is. Three models treated the low income as enough or wrongly put age 2 inside the preschool range. The fourth model applied the age cutoff correctly but still submitted a value of 1.

A 2-year-old qualifies for Medicaid through the age-based YOUNG_CHILD MAGI category, whose North Carolina income standard for ages 1-5 exceeds 200% FPL; this household sits at 0.58 x FPL, so the income test is satisfied outright. The trap is that Medicaid, unlike CHIP, imposes no bar on children who already hold employer-sponsored insurance, and it requires no disability, SSI, or other special categorical status beyond age. All three wrong answers refused the category: one swapped in CHIP's other-coverage exclusion, one measured the child against an adult-level FPL cutoff, and one defaulted to 0 for want of an extra eligibility flag that the children's pathway never requires.

WIC eligibility for a child turns on two things only: falling in the child category (age 1 through the fifth birthday) and household income at or below 185% of the federal poverty guideline, with adjunctive eligibility through Medicaid, SNAP, or TANF as an independent qualifying path. This three-person North Carolina household has at most $17,100 of self-employment income against a 185% FPL limit near $49,000 for 2026, so the income screen is cleared with enormous margin, and the head's listed WIC receipt reflects a household already certified under that same screen. Both wrong answers denied a child who satisfies the age category and the income test — one by inventing an income ceiling the household never approaches, the other by treating an unlisted enrollment flag as dispositive of eligibility.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

For a self-employed filer, earned income for both the EITC and the ACTC is SE profit minus the deduction for half of SE tax: $17,100 − ($17,100 × 0.9235 × 0.153 / 2 = $1,208.07) = $15,891.93. That amount is still in the two-child EITC phase-in, so the EITC is 40% × $15,891.93 = $6,356.77. Because regular tax is $0, the refundable CTC is 15% × ($15,891.93 − $2,500) = $2,008.79. The $2,500 floor was made permanent by OBBBA, and the result is below the $1,700-per-child cap. Most models went wrong in one of three ways: they used the wrong earned-income base (gross $17,100, the 92.35% net-earnings figure of $15,791.85, or a double-reduced $14,584); they used the expired $3,000 ACTC threshold or the $1,000-per-child CTC; or they dropped one of the two credits entirely.

The decisive step is the free-meal income test: $17,100 of self-employment income for a household of three is 63% of the federal poverty guideline, less than half the 130% ceiling for free meals, and the household is independently categorically eligible through SNAP ($524.80/month), which by itself confers free-meal status for the 10-year-old K-12 student. NC has no universal free school meal program, so the household qualifies through the standard free tier rather than a statewide waiver, and PolicyEngine values the benefit at $7.15/day for one enrolled child ($1,130.96/year). Both wrong models denied eligibility for a household at less than one-third of the free-meal income limit — one by asserting the income exceeded the threshold, the other by treating the absence of an explicit eligibility flag in the prompt as a negative.

The head is a 40-year-old living with two of their own children, which places them in the parent/caretaker-relative Medicaid category (medicaid_category = PARENT), a mandatory MAGI pathway that exists in every state independent of expansion status. Their only income is $17,100 of self-employment earnings, which after the deductible half of SE tax gives MAGI at 0.58 x FPL for a household of three — far below both the parent/caretaker limit and the 138% FPL adult limit North Carolina adopted when it implemented expansion on December 1, 2023 (S.L. 2023-7), in force for 2026. Every wrong model either declared the head a childless/non-categorical adult despite two listed children, or asserted NC is still a non-expansion state, and so answered 0 on a household that clears the income test by a wide margin on two independent pathways.

WIC eligibility depends on a person's own category: pregnant, postpartum (up to 6 months after delivery), breastfeeding (up to 12 months), infant, or child under 5. Low income alone doesn't qualify anyone. The head is a 40-year-old adult with no pregnancy flag, and the youngest child is 2, so the postpartum and breastfeeding windows ended long ago. The head therefore fits no WIC category, and only Child 2 is eligible. The 'receives wic' fact is a receipt/take-up input and does not make anyone eligible. Every model treated that receipt flag, or the head's role as parent of a child under 5, as a pathway to eligibility.

Employee payroll tax applies to wages, not SSTB self-employment income; that income instead enters the separate self-employment-tax calculation. With no reported wages and all unlisted numeric inputs set to zero, every component of the requested employee-side payroll tax is zero.

Reduced-price eligibility is mutually exclusive with the superior free-meals tier in this output. The household is in the FREE tier because it meets categorical eligibility through SNAP or TANF and its school-meal income is 63% of the federal poverty guideline, below the 130% free-meals threshold; therefore reduced-price support is zero.

This is a plain SECA calculation. Net SE earnings are $17,100 × 0.9235 = $15,791.85, which is far below the Social Security wage base, so the full 15.3% applies: $15,791.85 × 0.153 = $2,416.15. Every model either picked the right method and then made an arithmetic or rounding slip, or worked out about $2,416 and then submitted some other number. Two models subtracted things that do not reduce SE tax at all, such as the deduction for half of SE tax, which only lowers income-tax AGI.

The household has $1,425/month of gross self-employment earnings. Its net income is $931 after the $285 earned income deduction (20%) and the FY2026 $209 standard deduction for three people. The expected contribution is 30% of $931, rounded up to $280, and the $785 three-person maximum minus $280 gives $505/month, or $6,060 a year. The models split into four groups of errors: (1) models that used the right inputs but did not round the contribution up, getting $505.70 ($6,068.40) or $506 ($6,072); (2) models that used stale or invented maximum allotments and standard deductions from FY2024, FY2025, or rough projections; (3) models that wrongly reduced self-employment income by SE tax or by a 40% cost allowance; (4) models that zeroed out the benefit by applying a resource limit, which North Carolina's broad-based categorical eligibility through TANF non-cash eligibility waives.

Two independent paths lead to $0 of North Carolina tax. First, the only income fact listed is the SSTB *component* input; total self-employment income is unlisted and therefore 0 under the prompt's "treat any unlisted numeric input as 0" rule, so the engine's trace shows essentially no income entering nc_income_tax. Second, even crediting the full $17,100 as net self-employment earnings, federal AGI is $17,100 − $1,208 (half of SE tax) = $15,892, and North Carolina's 2026 head-of-household standard deduction of $19,125 — the head has two qualifying children — exceeds that, driving NC taxable income to $0 and the 3.99% 2026 flat rate onto a zero base. Every wrong model produced a positive liability; two of them derived exactly $0 in their own reasoning and then submitted a different number anyway.

The 2026 result follows OBBBA law. AGI is $156,275.86, with 85% of Social Security taxable. The filer takes the $18,150 standard deduction ($16,100 base plus $2,050 aged add-on). The $6,000 senior deduction phases down by 6% of MAGI above $75,000, leaving $1,123.45. The new §170(p) charitable deduction for non-itemizers adds $1,000 for a single filer. That leaves taxable income of $136,002.41, taxed at the OBBBA-reset brackets (10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700, then 24%). The closest models handled everything except the $1,000 non-itemizer charitable deduction and came out exactly $240 high. A large group applied TCJA-sunset law (personal exemption, 15/25/28% brackets), which OBBBA repealed. Others left out the senior deduction, did not phase it out, or used inflation-projected parameters.

The only FICA-taxable income here is the $83,635 of wages: the $67,760 taxable pension and $5,742 Social Security retirement benefit are outside the payroll tax base, the wage is far below the 2026 Social Security wage base, age 70 does not exempt wages from FICA, and Florida levies no mandatory employee state payroll tax. The answer is therefore exactly 6.2% × $83,635 = $5,185.37 plus 1.45% × $83,635 = $1,212.71, or $6,398.08. What separates the reference from the wrong answers is execution of that single multiplication at the employee-side rate: two models stated the right rule and then mis-multiplied or rounded, one submitted a number contradicting its own correct explanation, one used the combined 12.4%/2.9% employer-plus-employee rates before guessing, and one submitted a placeholder zero.

The HSA deduction and other applicable adjustments reduce adjusted gross income to -$5,882.05, and taxable income remains zero after the standard deduction. With zero income tax before credits and no other included tax components, federal income tax before refundable credits is $0.

New Jersey’s ACA expansion covers this 20-year-old as a MAGI-based adult because the person satisfies the immigration rule and the engine’s MAGI income level is 0.00 times FPL. Employer-sponsored insurance does not disqualify an otherwise eligible adult from Medicaid; it affects other health-coverage calculations, including ACA premium assistance. The wrong answers either imposed that nonexistent ESI exclusion or replaced the Medicaid MAGI calculation with a sum of inputs that the engine does not count as MAGI in that manner.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Employee payroll tax applies to wage earnings, and the household has no reported wages or salary. The listed SSTB self-employment income belongs in the separately requested self-employment-tax calculation, while alimony and financial assistance are not employee FICA wages.

Self-employment tax applies because $4,340 exceeds the $400 filing threshold. Multiplying the 92.35% net-earnings base by the combined 15.3% Social Security and Medicare rate yields $613.22; the threshold does not reduce the taxable base or eliminate liability.

Gross income counts the $12,000 financial assistance as unearned income, giving $1,486.54/month: $361.67 self-employment, $124.92 alimony and $1,000 assistance. That is 112% of FPL, well under NJ's broad-based categorical eligibility limit. After the $213.68 standard deduction and the $72.33 earned-income deduction, adjusted income is $1,200.53. Shelter costs are only the $995.75/month real estate taxes. Home mortgage interest is a tax-deduction input and is not a SNAP shelter cost here, so the excess shelter deduction is an uncapped $395.49 and net income is $805.04. The formula benefit is $304.68 − $241.50 = $63.18, which New Jersey's $95 state minimum benefit replaces, giving $1,140 a year. Models went wrong in four ways: they excluded the assistance, counted mortgage interest and hit the shelter cap, declared the household ineligible, or zeroed out a sub-maximum formula without applying the NJ $95 floor. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (categorical_eligibility). The frozen reference is 1,140.00; the alternative is 0.00. The prompt lists no hours worked and says to treat unlisted numeric inputs as 0; the reference assumed 40 hours a week, which clears the SNAP work requirement for able-bodied adults without dependents. Under the zero-hours reading the time limit applies, which ends benefits after three countable months unless an exemption or area waiver applies; the alternative value is the engine's zero-hours result, not a certified entitlement. The prompt also lists home mortgage interest without saying the mortgaged home is the household's residence; if it is, SNAP counts the mortgage payment, interest included, as a shelter cost (7 CFR 273.9(d)(6)(ii)(A)), which is the reading under the alternative value. Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (weekly_hours_worked_before_lsr and whether the listed home mortgage interest is on the home the SNAP household occupies).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

New Jersey's gross income tax exempts a single filer entirely when New Jersey gross income falls at or below the $10,000 minimum filing threshold, and this household's NJ gross income is $5,838.53 (alimony $1,498.53 plus self-employment $4,340.00; the $12,000 of financial assistance is not NJ gross income). PolicyEngine therefore computes the bracket tax as an intermediate figure — $4,838.53 of taxable income after the $1,000 regular exemption, times the 1.4% first-bracket rate, equals $67.74 — and then zeroes it out under the below-threshold exemption, leaving $0.00. Every wrong model stopped at the 1.4% bracket arithmetic and never applied the threshold exemption; three of them also mis-specified the NJ income and deduction base along the way.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine's NJ EITC formula for childless filers aged 18 to 24 caps the unscaled $308.55 federal-formula phase-in amount at 40% of the $664 2026 federal maximum ($265.60). N.J.S.A. 54A:4-7 instead requires 40% of the full federal-formula credit, which gives 0.40 × $308.55 = $123.42.
case_annotation: The deciding rule is that New Jersey gives its refundable EITC to filers aged 18 and over who have no qualifying children. It is computed with the federal formula even though the federal childless credit requires age 25. Most models tied NJ eligibility to federal eligibility or to an outdated age-21 floor, and returned $0 or a $50 property-tax credit. EITC earned income here is $4,340 minus half of SE tax ($306.61), which is $4,033.39, so the phase-in amount is $308.55. Models that applied NJ's 40% match to that amount got $123.42. The reference's $265.60 equals 40% of the $664 2026 maximum childless credit, which the engine reaches by capping the $308.55 phase-in amount at that scaled maximum. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_engine_defect; adjudicated llm_error (credit_phaseout). New Jersey bases the earned income credit for filers 18 and older who fail only the federal age test on the federal maximum credit for filers without a qualifying child, and pays it as a flat yearly amount: 40% of the 2026 $664 maximum is $265.60. The judge's phase-in reading fails. Reference affirmed (N.J.S.A. 54A:4-7(a)(4); Rev. Proc. 2025-32).

TANF is categorically limited to assistance units containing a dependent child: New Jersey's WorkFirst NJ/TANF requires a needy child under 18 (or 18 and a full-time secondary student) in the unit, and childless adults are served instead by WFNJ General Assistance, which is not TANF. This household is a single 20-year-old head with no children, so the benefit is $0 regardless of the income test. The second trap is that `financial_assistance` is an input income line in the household facts, not a computed program output; echoing it back as the TANF benefit both invents categorical eligibility and confuses an input with the requested computed value.

The household's only refundable credit is the no-qualifying-child EITC, and it gets the full 2026 maximum of $664. The joint return passes the age test because one spouse, the head at 43, is between 25 and 64; only one spouse has to qualify. Earned income is about $9,665: $10,400 of self-employment income minus the deductible half of self-employment tax. That is above the 2026 phase-in ceiling of about $8,680 and well below the married-filing-jointly phase-out start of about $18,000, so the credit sits on the plateau. Models split two ways. Some denied the credit outright, citing the age test, treating self-employment income as non-earned, or claiming the household was in the phase-out. The rest found the plateau but used a stale or mis-indexed maximum ($649 for 2025, or $666–$667) or made arithmetic and phase-out errors.

The head is blind and disabled, with very low countable income ($10,400 of self-employment income, $14 of disability benefits) and only $912 in assets. That makes the head an SSI recipient, receiving about $7,231 a year. Louisiana gives automatic Medicaid to SSI recipients, so the engine puts the head in the SSI_RECIPIENT category. The head would also qualify under Louisiana's adult expansion, because household MAGI is only 0.45× FPL, far below the 138% limit. All four models missed the SSI pathway, and none of them checked the head's income against the expansion limit correctly.

Before 65, a person qualifies for Medicare only after 24 months of Social Security disability (SSDI) entitlement, or through the ESRD/ALS pathways. PolicyEngine checks this with months of Social Security disability receipt, and it does not use the is_disabled or is_blind flags. The head is 43. Their only disability income is $14 of generic "disability benefits", which is not Social Security disability. No months of SSDI receipt are listed, so that input is 0, and neither ESRD nor ALS is listed either. Every model treated disability status plus a nominal disability-benefit amount as enough for Medicare under 65. That skips both the SSDI-entitlement requirement and the 24-month waiting period.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The whole case reduces to one canonical computation: net earnings from self-employment are 92.35% of the $10,400 SSTB profit ($9,604.40), and the combined OASDI/HI rate of 15.3% applies in full because $9,604.40 is far under the 2026 Social Security wage base, giving 0.153 × 9,604.40 = $1,469.47. The $400 figure in §1402(b) is the floor at which SE tax begins, not a ceiling below which it is waived, and no other floor exists; the one-half-of-SE-tax figure is an above-the-line deduction under §164(f), not the liability. The prompt further defines this output as SE tax excluding Additional Medicare Tax, and the 0.9% AMT threshold for joint filers is $250,000 of combined earnings, so nothing is added on top. Every wrong answer comes from inverting the $400 floor, inventing a different floor, truncating the 0.9235 base factor, reporting the deduction instead of the tax, or bolting on a nonexistent AMT.

The trap is the SSI amount, which must be counted as unearned income for SNAP. The engine gives the head $602.58/month of SSI: the individual rate of $994 minus $391.42 of countable income ($866.67 of self-employment income, minus the leftover $18.83 general exclusion and the $65 earned-income exclusion, then halved). Monthly SNAP gross income is therefore $866.67 + $3.17 + $602.58 = $1,472.42. Subtracting the 20% earned-income deduction ($173.33) and the $209 standard deduction leaves net income of $1,090.08, so the benefit is $546 − $327 = $219/month for January–September. October–December use FY2027 parameters ($558.24 − $325.50 = $232.74/month), for a total of $2,669.22. Roughly half the models left SSI out of SNAP income and got about $4,700. Most of the others counted SSI at the couple rate of about $1,099/month and got about $840. The rest called the household ineligible or produced unsupported numbers. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 2669.217041 to 883.617065 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. Moves with the additional SSI counted as household income. The 2026-09-22 audit recomputes the alternative as 840.00 with every publication convention and upstream fix (the frozen-engine value above was 883.62). Reference depends on an unlisted input; output excluded from scoring (42 U.S.C. 1382c(a)(3)(A); 20 CFR 416.905).

CHIP requires the person to be outside Medicaid eligibility; a low income alone does not establish CHIP eligibility. The spouse is Medicaid-eligible in Louisiana's adult category, so the Medicaid exclusion makes `spouse_chip_eligible` false without applying a CHIP income threshold.

Louisiana adopted the ACA adult expansion effective July 1, 2016, so any non-elderly adult aged 19–64 who is not otherwise eligible qualifies for Medicaid on income alone at or below 138% FPL under MAGI methodology — no pregnancy, parenthood, or disability category is required. The spouse is 20 with household MAGI at 0.45 x FPL (the only income is the head's $10,400 SSTB self-employment plus $38 of disability benefits, against a two-person 2026 FPL near $21,150 and a 138% cutoff near $29,200), placing the household roughly a third of the way to the expansion limit. Every wrong model either invented an income excess that does not exist or applied pre-ACA categorical gatekeeping that Louisiana abolished, and each therefore returned 0 where the ADULT expansion pathway returns eligible.

To be eligible for Medicare before age 65, a person must be entitled to Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) and have received it for 24 months, or have ESRD or ALS.
