Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 32(c)(2)(A)(i), 24(d)(1)(B)(i), 402(e)(3); Cal. R&TC 17052(c)(4)(A)).

Free school meals are awarded through two independent pathways, and this Montana household clears both: it receives $8,625.89 of SNAP, which categorically confers free-meal status, and its countable income of $11,979.68 ($5,914.72 wages plus $6,064.96 TANF) is 44% of the federal poverty guideline for a three-person household, far under the 130% free-meal ceiling. The two children, ages 5 and 6, are both school-age, so the free tier pays a $7.15 daily per-child subsidy for the contiguous-US school year, $2,261.92 annually. The trap is that SNAP and TANF receipt are derived outputs of this same household, not listed input facts, so a model that only credits explicitly stated benefit receipt loses the categorical pathway — but even the wage-only figure of $5,915 sits at roughly 22% of the poverty guideline, so the income test alone still lands in the free tier. Both models returned 0 without running either test.

The head is a 46-year-old parent of two young children with MAGI of about $5,915, which is 0.07 × FPL for a household of three. That is far below Montana's Medicaid limit for the parent/caretaker category, so the head is eligible. MAGI-based Medicaid has no asset test, and having employer-sponsored insurance does not bar eligibility. The wrong models used an invented FPL dollar figure, applied an asset test, or treated ESI as disqualifying. None of them compared 7% of FPL against the parent income limit.

Medicare eligibility below age 65 does not follow from a current disability flag alone; it requires a qualifying Medicare pathway, such as entitlement after the applicable Social Security disability waiting period or eligibility based on end-stage renal disease. The 46-year-old head has no listed Medicare-qualifying entitlement or condition, so the disability input does not change the result from ineligible.

WIC eligibility is individual, not household-wide: an adult qualifies only as a pregnant, breastfeeding, or postpartum woman, while merely caring for a young child does not confer eligibility. The 46-year-old head has no qualifying WIC status, and neither low household income nor a child's presence satisfies the head's categorical requirement.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The trap is the payroll-tax wage base: PolicyEngine assesses employee OASDI at 6.2% and HI at 1.45% on the full $5,915 of employment income, giving $366.71 + $85.76 = $452.48. None of the listed health inputs touch that base — the $20,644 employer-sponsored insurance premium and the two $564 individually paid premiums are health-coverage and medical-expense inputs, not Section 125 salary reductions — and the $710 FLSA overtime premium is already inside the annual gross wage figure rather than additional to it. Traditional 401(k) and IRA amounts also leave FICA wages untouched, and Montana imposes no mandatory employee-side state payroll tax, so the answer is exactly 7.65% of wages. The wrong answers split into base errors (subtracting premiums to $4,787 or to $0, or adding the overtime premium to reach $6,625) and, for the three models that found the right base, an arithmetic slip, an invented rounding, and a value/explanation mismatch.

Reduced-price eligibility is mutually exclusive with the superior free-meals tier. This household is at 44% of the federal poverty guideline and also meets categorical eligibility, so its school_meal_tier is FREE and reduced_price_school_meals_eligible is 0.

SNAP gross income is $998.31 a month: $492.92 in wages plus about $505.39 in Montana TANF cash, which counts as unearned income. The deductions are the $209 standard deduction, the $98.58 earned income deduction (20%), and a $453.64 excess shelter deduction. The shelter deduction comes from Montana's standard utility allowance, which counts as a shelter cost even though no rent is listed. There is no excess medical deduction because the head receives no disability benefit such as SSI or Social Security disability, so the head does not count as disabled for SNAP. Net income is $237.09, and 30% of that ($71.10) is subtracted from the maximum allotment. That gives $713.90 a month for January–September and $733.60 for October–December, when the FY2027 allotment of $802.60 applies. Most models used wages only, left out TANF, added a medical deduction, and landed near the maximum allotment ($9,000–$9,420). The models that counted TANF left out the shelter deduction and landed around $7,000–$7,800. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 8625.889648 to 8917.490234 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. SSI stays $0 under either reading ($2,800 in the bank exceeds the $2,000 resource limit); SNAP moves through the elderly-or-disabled SNAP rules. The 2026-09-22 audit recomputes the alternative as 8,844.00 with every publication convention and upstream fix (the frozen-engine value above was 8,917.49). r30_snap_heat_and_eat_sua (engine defect, not fixed upstream) also moves this output on the stated facts, from 8,556.00 to 6,924.00; the record keeps its 2026-09-05 classification.

The generic `is disabled` household fact does not make the head categorically eligible for SSI under PolicyEngine; the controlling SSI-specific indicator is `is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled=False`. All three individuals fail the aged-65-or-older, blind, or qualifying-disabled requirement, so income exclusions, resources, and benefit-rate calculations are never reached and household SSI is $0.

Montana's state refundable credits for this household come only from the Montana EITC. For 2026 that credit is refundable and equals 20% of the federal EITC. The federal EITC is the 40% two-child phase-in rate applied to the head's full $5,915 of earned income, which gives $2,365.89, so the Montana credit is $473.18. Most models went wrong in one of three ways: they said Montana has no state EITC, no income tax, or only a nonrefundable EITC (giving $0); they used the older 3% or 10% rate; or they cut earned income by the $3,859 traditional 401(k) deferral, which gives a federal EITC of $822.40. A few also added a $1,200 young-child credit that PolicyEngine does not count in this household's Montana refundable credits. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (credit_phaseout). The frozen reference is 473.18; the corrected value is 164.46. PolicyEngine counts elective 401(k) deferrals as earned income for the EITC and refundable child tax credit. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 32(c)(2)(A)(i), 24(d)(1)(B)(i), 402(e)(3); Cal. R&TC 17052(c)(4)(A)).

The family of three qualifies for Montana TANF. Its $2,800 in bank assets is under the $3,000 resource limit, and the one vehicle is excluded. The head gets no SSI because $2,800 is over the $2,000 SSI resource limit, so there is no unearned income to count. Countable earnings are 0.75 × ($5,915/12 − $200) = $219.69 a month, after the $200 disregard plus 25% of the rest. That amount is subtracted from Montana's 2026 three-person payment standard of about $725.10 a month, which gives about $505.41 a month, or $6,064.96 a year. Most wrong answers either returned $0 by inventing reasons the family was ineligible (no modeling, asset limits that are too low, SSI receipt, or counting overtime twice) or used an outdated payment standard around $588 or a 50% earnings disregard.

The correct path is: AGI of $101,130 ($103,000 wages minus the $1,870 capital loss; the pension and veterans benefits are not taxable), minus the $16,100 2026 single standard deduction and nothing else, gives taxable income of $85,030. Under the 2026 brackets that OBBBA made permanent (10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, then 22%), that is $1,240 + $4,560 + $7,618.60 = $13,418.60, with no nonrefundable credits. The wrong answers fall into three groups. One group applied the TCJA-sunset rules ($8,300 standard deduction plus a $5,300 personal exemption, with 15%/25% brackets). A second group used 2025 or guessed standard deductions and bracket thresholds. A third group subtracted the $1,400 auto loan interest even though nothing in the facts shows a qualified passenger vehicle loan. Several models reached $13,418.60 or $85,030 and then reported a different number.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The correct calculation is simple. Employee Social Security is 6.2% of the full $103,000 of wages, or $6,386, because the wages are below the 2026 wage base. Employee Medicare is 1.45%, or $1,493.50. No Additional Medicare Tax applies below $200,000, and Texas has no employee state payroll tax, so the total is $7,879.50. Most models reached exactly $7,879.50 in their reasoning and then submitted a different number with a made-up "adjustment." One model treated the listed health insurance premiums as a pre-tax payroll exclusion, another submitted zero, and one gave no output.

Texas imposes no individual state income tax, so a Texas resident has $0 of state income tax before refundable credits regardless of the listed taxable-income deductions or credits. Taxes from other jurisdictions do not apply because the household resides in Texas.

OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent, so 2026 uses a $32,200 MFJ standard deduction and a 10% bracket that ends at $24,800. Gross income is $87,201 and the QBI deduction is $0.20, so taxable income is $55,000.80. The tax is then $2,480 + 12% × $30,200.80 = $6,104.10, and no nonrefundable credits apply. The listed wages already are the gross amounts, so the $7,989 employer-sponsored insurance premium is not subtracted from them. Most models either used pre-OBBBA inflation projections ($30,000–$30,840 standard deduction with a $23,850–$24,500 bracket), assumed the TCJA had expired and used personal exemptions with a 15% bracket, wrongly excluded the ESI premium, or reported a final number that did not match their own math.

Refundable federal credits require a qualifying statutory pathway; disability alone does not create a refundable federal income tax credit. With no qualifying children, education expenses, or other credit-triggering facts, and income above the childless EITC range, every refundable component is zero.

Disability alone does not establish North Carolina Medicaid eligibility; the person must qualify through a specific MAGI or traditional categorical pathway and satisfy that pathway's financial rules. The head's household MAGI is $87,201, or 4.03 times FPL, and the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE, so medical expenses, rent, and $1,001 in assets do not create eligibility.

Under age 65, a disability flag alone does not make someone eligible for Medicare. The disability route requires 24 months of Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) entitlement, or end-stage renal disease or ALS. The household reports no SSDI income, and the head earns $41,200 in wages, far above substantial gainful activity. So the only pathway PolicyEngine can apply is the age-65 test, and a 26-year-old fails it. Every model treated the 'is disabled' flag as enough for Medicare and skipped the SSDI-duration requirement.

The reference applies the 6.2% employee Social Security rate and the 1.45% Medicare rate to each spouse's full listed gross wages: $41,200 and $46,000. That gives 7.65% × $87,200 = $6,670.80. Neither spouse reaches the Social Security wage base, combined wages are far below the $250,000 joint threshold for Additional Medicare Tax, and NC has no employee state payroll tax. The most common mistake was subtracting the spouse's $7,989 employer-sponsored insurance premium from FICA wages as if it were a Section 125 salary reduction, which gives $6,059.64. Most of the other wrong models reached $6,670.80 in their reasoning and then submitted a different number because of arithmetic, rounding or transcription errors.

Self-employment tax applies only when net earnings from self-employment reach the filing threshold; the head’s listed $1 produces no liability. There is no minimum $31 self-employment tax or rounding rule that converts this de minimis amount into a positive tax.

Under-65 Medicare eligibility does not come from a bare disability flag. It requires 24 months of Social Security Disability Insurance entitlement, or end-stage renal disease or ALS. The spouse is 26, receives no SSDI (the benefit is unlisted, so it is $0), and has no ESRD or ALS, so only the age-65 test applies and it fails. All seven models used the same made-up shortcut, "disabled = Medicare eligible," and skipped the SSDI 24-month entitlement step.

North Carolina taxes 2026 income at a flat 3.99%. The base is federal AGI of $87,201 ($87,200 in wages plus $1 of self-employment income) minus the fixed $25,500 joint standard deduction, which gives $61,701 and $2,461.87 of tax. Most models went wrong in one of two ways. Some used an outdated or invented rate (4.25%, 4.5%, 4%, 4.49%) or a wrong standard deduction ($21,500, $23,400, $23,850, $26,400, $30,000). CHIP is limited to children who do not qualify for Medicaid. At approximately $30,000 of household income, the age-9 child qualifies for Florida Medicaid in the OLDER_CHILD category, so Medicaid eligibility precludes CHIP eligibility even though the income is below CHIP's upper limit.

Florida's refusal of adult Medicaid expansion does not touch children's coverage: the state's mandatory MAGI pathway for the older-child category (ages 6-18) runs to 133% FPL, and a 9-year-old in a household of five with roughly $21,600 of MAGI sits at 0.72 FPL — barely half the threshold. The only computation required is household MAGI from the $30,000 of self-employment income divided by the family-of-five poverty guideline, then compared with 133% FPL; no asset test, no enrollment fact, and no SSI linkage enters the children's MAGI pathway. Both models returned 0 without ever running that ratio, treating Medicaid eligibility as something the prompt had to assert rather than something the stated income and age determine.

CHIP eligibility requires the child to be ineligible for Medicaid, not merely under age 19 and below CHIP's upper income limit. At age 6 and this household income, child2 qualifies for Medicaid under Florida's OLDER_CHILD category, so the Medicaid–CHIP mutual-exclusivity rule makes child2 ineligible for CHIP.

Head Start eligibility requires satisfying the program’s preschool-age and income rules. Child 2 is age 6, and the household’s approximately $30,000 annual income exceeds the applicable Head Start income threshold in the PolicyEngine calculation; no foster-care or qualifying-assistance exception applies.

The trap is Florida's older-child Medicaid pathway: children ages 6-18 are covered up to 133% FPL, a MAGI category with no asset test and no dependence on the state's refusal to expand adult coverage. With $30,000 of self-employment income for a household of five, MAGI lands at 0.72 x FPL, about half the applicable limit, so child2 qualifies under OLDER_CHILD. All three models conflated Florida's non-expansion posture (which closes only the adult pathway) or a stale 100% FPL children's threshold with the child MAGI test, and each returned 0 on income that clears the real limit with wide margin.

WIC child eligibility ends at the fifth birthday, so a six-year-old cannot qualify through the infant-or-child category regardless of household income. Child 2 is age 6 and has no listed pregnancy or postpartum status, leaving no WIC categorical eligibility pathway.

The newborn satisfies the under-age-3 rule, and the five-person household's $30,000 annual income satisfies the benchmark's income test, so the child is eligible.

The dispositive rule is Florida's age-based INFANT Medicaid category, which covers children under age 1 at MAGI up to 185% FPL — a far higher threshold than the adult standards, and one that applies in a non-expansion state. The household's MAGI is 0.72 FPL, so the only two conditions that matter, age under 1 and income under the infant threshold, are both satisfied. All three models denied eligibility by routing the infant through adult or generic standards: one gave no derivation, one required an SSI/disability-style marker that MAGI categories do not use, and one computed the income test correctly and then overrode it with a nonexistent asset test plus a Medicaid-expansion and enrollment requirement.

WIC eligibility is derived from the child's age and household income; it does not require the prompt to explicitly state that the child is WIC-eligible. Child 3 is under age five, and the household's approximately $30,000 annual income is below the 2026 WIC limit of 185% of the federal poverty guideline for a five-person household.

The 2026 married-filing-jointly standard deduction does not reduce this household's taxable income to zero after the deductible half of self-employment tax. The FREE tier here is over-determined: the household's $8,020.55 SNAP benefit confers categorical free-meal eligibility outright, and independently $30,000 for a five-person household is 78% of the federal poverty guideline, far under the 130% free-meal cutoff. Most models that used current 2026 law included estate income in a $169,943 AGI, pushed ordinary income into the 24% bracket, and landed near $25,750–$25,841. The applicable standard deduction eliminates taxable income, so the tax computation yields $0; both models expressly derived zero taxable income and zero liability but then submitted unsupported positive amounts.

At 72, the head is outside the ACA expansion-adult category, which covers ages 19–64 up to 138% FPL. Their MAGI is also about 202% FPL, so that pathway fails twice. The head gets no SSI, so the SSI-recipient route is closed. The aged/blind/disabled route has an income limit near the SSI/100% FPL level, roughly $1,000–$1,300 a month. The head's unearned income is about $3,637 a month, so it is far over that limit even after the $20 general disregard. All four models treated being aged, blind or disabled plus low assets as enough to qualify and skipped the income test, which leaves medicaid_category = NONE.

Employee payroll taxes apply to covered wages and other employment compensation, not Social Security retirement benefits or taxable IRA distributions. Because neither spouse has wages or other employee compensation, the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory Washington employee payroll-tax bases are all zero, yielding $0.

Washington's 200% gross-income screening rule does not itself establish categorical SNAP eligibility or guarantee the minimum allotment. This two-person household's approximately $43,640 annual income disqualifies it, so the minimum-benefit rule never applies and annual SNAP equals $0.

The spouse is 49, so their only Medicaid routes are the MAGI adult-expansion group and the blind/disabled pathway. For Medicaid, MAGI adds back non-taxable Social Security. The tax unit's MAGI is therefore the head's full $25,400 Social Security plus $18,240 in IRA distributions, or $43,640. That is 2.02x FPL, far above the 138% expansion limit. The blind/disabled pathway in PolicyEngine is not open-ended. It depends on SSI receipt or an SSI-related income test that counts the couple's combined income. The spouse gets $0 SSI because the head's income is deemed to them and wipes out the couple's SSI benefit. With no category reached, the engine returns medicaid_category NONE. Every model either treated blindness/disability as enough on its own, ignored spousal income, or left Social Security out of MAGI.

Under age 65, a person qualifies for Medicare through disability only after 24 months of entitlement to Social Security disability benefits (42 U.S.C. 426(b)), or through the ESRD or ALS pathways. PolicyEngine models the same rule: the age-65 test or at least 24 months of Social Security disability receipt. The spouse is 49 and flagged disabled, but the household lists no Social Security disability income, no months of SSDI receipt, and no ESRD or ALS, so the spouse fails every pathway. All ten models treated the disability flag alone as enough for Medicare. They skipped the separate requirement of 24 months of SSDI entitlement.

The trap is the $13,000 "financial assistance" line: in PolicyEngine `financial_assistance` is a non-taxable cash receipt (counted for benefit means-tests, never in gross income or AGI), so the only taxable items here are $5,923 of wages and $1,920 of farm rent income, reduced by the $3,000 capital-loss limitation on the -$9,944 long-term loss, for AGI of roughly $4,843. That sits far below the 2026 single standard deduction (~$16,100), leaving taxable income of $0, no NIIT (net investment income is a $3,000 loss), and no add-on liabilities, hence $0. Both models handled the $3,000 capital-loss cap and the standard deduction correctly but pushed the $13,000 gift/assistance through as ordinary income, manufacturing $1,743 of taxable income and a $174.30 bracket tax. Excluding the non-taxable transfer collapses the entire computation to zero.

The head is 31, has no qualifying children, and has $5,923 of wage earnings, so they qualify for the childless EITC. That credit phases in at 7.65% of earned income starting from the first dollar: 7.65% × $5,923 ≈ $453.10. AGI is $5,923 + $1,920 − $3,000 (the capital-loss cap) = $4,843, which is below the phase-out start. The $1,920 of farm rent is far below the investment-income limit. No other refundable credit applies. Most models went wrong in one of three ways: they wrongly ruled out the childless EITC at low earnings, they subtracted the $8,389 employer-insurance premium from wages to get zero earned income, or they worked out about $453 and then changed it to some other number without a valid reason.

Texas does not provide MAGI Medicaid eligibility to a nondependent, childless 31-year-old merely because income is below an income threshold. The head meets the immigration requirement but belongs to none of Texas's active Medicaid categories, so the low 0.30-FPL MAGI level does not create eligibility.

WIC requires both financial eligibility and membership in a qualifying demographic category: pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding women, infants, or children under age five. The 31-year-old head has no listed qualifying status, and unlisted statuses are false, so passing the income test does not establish WIC eligibility.

Employer-sponsored insurance premiums are not automatically employee pre-tax cafeteria-plan deductions from FICA wages; the listed $5,923 remains subject to employee Social Security and Medicare taxes. PolicyEngine computes $367.22 of Social Security tax and $85.88 of Medicare tax, totaling $453.10, with no Additional Medicare Tax or mandatory Texas employee payroll tax.

Self-employment tax applies only to positive net earnings from self-employment, after determining the applicable self-employment tax base. The household’s relevant net income is approximately -$2,101, so there are no positive net self-employment earnings and the tax base is zero; treating the $1,920 farm rent entry as a standalone positive self-employment tax base produces the wrong liability.

PolicyEngine counts wages ($493.58/mo) and the $13,000 financial assistance ($1,083.33/mo) but not farm rent. That gives gross income of $1,576.90 (121% FPL, inside Texas's 165% FPL BBCE limit). SNAP eligibility uses approximately $23,442 of annual household income here: $18,708 of Social Security plus $4,734 of tax-exempt interest. Alabama follows its own income definition. It adds federally tax-exempt interest back into Alabama gross income because Alabama taxes interest on other states' municipal obligations. That puts this filer's Alabama AGI at $4,734, while the $18,708 of Social Security stays exempt. Alabama's single standard deduction is $3,000 at this income level, with no age-65 or disability add-on, and the personal exemption is $1,500, for $4,500 total. That leaves $234 of taxable income, taxed at 2% to give $4.68. Every model either dropped the interest from the Alabama tax base or overstated the deductions so they absorbed the full $4,734.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

SNAP’s minimum allotment applies only after a household passes the program’s eligibility tests; it cannot override failure of the gross-income test. At $52,800 of annual household income, this household exceeds the applicable 2026 gross-income limit, so the computation stops with no SNAP benefit.

Florida did not expand Medicaid, so a childless, non-pregnant 42-year-old has no MAGI adult or parent category, even with MAGI at 0% FPL (veterans benefits are left out of MAGI). Disability alone does not create eligibility. The disabled pathway requires either receiving SSI or passing Florida's aged/disabled income test. The spouse's $52,800 in veterans benefits counts as unearned income under SSI-related rules, which pushes SSI to $0 and puts the spouse far above the aged/disabled income limit, so medicaid_category is NONE. All three models treated disability status as enough to qualify and never applied the income test that comes with the disabled pathway.

Under age 65, Medicare eligibility comes only from 24 months of Social Security Disability Insurance (Title II) entitlement or from ESRD/ALS. A disability flag on its own does not confer it. The spouse is 42 and receives $52,800 in veterans benefits, which are VA payments and not SSDI. With SSDI income and SSDI months both unlisted, they are 0 under the prompt's rules, so the age test and the SSDI-duration test both fail. All four models treated "is disabled" (plus, for one model, VA benefits) as enough for disability-based Medicare, and so answered Yes.

Age alone does not establish Head Start eligibility; the child must also qualify through an applicable eligibility pathway, principally the program's low-income criteria in this case. The 2026 return for this married-filing-jointly household uses these rules: AGI of $250,733.36 (wages plus the taxable state refund minus the capital loss), and the full $25,000 OBBBA qualified-overtime deduction, because the joint phaseout starts at $300,000 MAGI. The refundable CTC (ACTC) is capped at the part of the child tax credit left over after the credit has offset income tax. This couple files jointly with about $250,733 of AGI. Their federal income tax is well over $25,000, which absorbs the whole $6,600 as a nonrefundable credit and leaves nothing to refund. EITC is zero at this income, and no other refundable credit applies, so the total is $0. The wrong answers skipped the tax-liability limit and treated the per-child refundable cap ($1,700 or $1,800), or a made-up fraction of it, as money the family receives automatically.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine's NY real property tax credit measures household gross income without nontaxable Social Security and SSI. Tax Law §606(e)(1) and Form IT-214 (line 10 Social Security; line 12 public assistance/SSI) include both. That puts this 65+ filer in the ≤$1,000 band with the $375 cap. Counting the $2,800 of Social Security alone gives the $2,001–$3,000 band and a $341 cap, and adding SSI gives the $12,001–$13,000 band and a $171 cap.
case_annotation: The whole amount comes from New York's real property tax credit (IT-214, Tax Law §606(e)). It is a refundable circuit-breaker credit for homeowners and renters with household gross income of $18,000 or less, and it is paid even when the filer owes no tax. For a 74-year-old homeowner paying about $1,634 in property taxes against almost no income, the property taxes are far above the income-based threshold, so the 65+ maximum caps the credit at $375. Most models only checked the EITC and child credits, assumed a refundable credit needs tax liability or rent, or dismissed homeowners. The rest used the under-65 cap, added the nonrefundable household credit, made up a formula, or used a lower income band by counting Social Security and SSI. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (state_local_rule). From 2025 New York keys the real property tax credit to federal AGI and a flat table; with federal AGI of $0 and property tax above 3.5% of it, a filer 65 or older receives $375. The judge applied the repealed household-gross-income rule. Reference affirmed (N.Y. Tax Law 606(e) as amended by Part RR of Chapter 59 of the Laws of 2025).

For 2026, OBBBA keeps the TCJA structure. The CDCC rate at this AGI is 35%, giving $546. Tax before credits is $3,056.23. The CDCC and the $200 Saver's credit bring it down to $2,310.23. reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine's EITC uses the full $55,000 of gross wages as earned income: 7,316 − 0.2106 × (55,000 − 23,890) = 764.23. Models missed by zeroing the EITC, assuming tax absorbed the whole CTC, using a $2,000 or $1,000 per-child CTC, applying the old 20% CDCC rate, omitting the Saver's Credit, subtracting employer insurance premiums from AGI, using the wrong filing status, or phasing out the EITC on AGI.
